lawyer:
Salma Rahman Assistant Attorney-General with Towhida Khatun Assistant Attorney-General—For the Petitioners. 
Rezina Mahmud, Advocate—For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Bangladesh and others ------Petitioners 
Vs.
Abdul Aziz ------Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule under section 11 of the Code of Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of defendants respondents-petitioners calls in question the judgment and decree dated 4-5-2008 passed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria in Title Appeal No. 61 of 2006 by which the learned District Judge, allowed the appeal on contest by setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria on 30-4-2006 in Title Suit No. 110 of 2005 decreeing the suit.

2. The short facts which have given rise to the Rule are as follows: the opposite party as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 110 of 2005 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria praying for declaration of his title over the suit property mentioned in the schedule of the plaint.

3. The plaintiff in the plaint had stated, inter alia that Bishnu Kapali was the original owner of the suit jote and he died leaving behind a son Nagarbashi Kapali and a daughter Ananta Bala who became the successors of Bishnu Kapali who sold the suit property by two registered deeds dated 22-12-2951 AD to Moezuddin @ Darag Ali the father of the plaintiff and Mongal Miah, the paternal uncle of the plaintiff; that Mondal Miah had no issue and thus Moezuddin @ Darag Ali became owner of the suit property; that SA khatian was rightly recorded in the name of the Darag Ali @ Moezuddin; that the plaintiff got some of the suit land mutated in his name in SA khatian and that he paid rent of the suit property including other properties till 2001 to the government . It is further stated that the suit property was wrongly recorded in the filed khatian in the name of the government during last settlement survey which created cloud in the title of the plaintiff over the suit property. As such the plaintiff has been compelled to file the instant suit.

4. The government contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation stated in the plaint that the suit is barred by limitation and also barred by principle of estoppel, acquiescence and waiver and that the suit is not maintainable and the suit is false and fabricated. The registered deeds of the plaintiff were fake and fraudulent. The suit property was rightly recorded in the name of the Government during last settlement survey. It is further stated that the real facts of the case is that SA record was prepared in the name of Mahananda Kapali, son of Govinda Kapali in khatian No. 111 and that an area of 70 decimals land had been recorded in the name of Darag Ali in khatian No. 13 and another 57 decimals had been recorded in the name of nine others and, as such, an area of 1.27 acres was recorded in SA khatian and, as such, total area of land does not match. It is also stated that record of Tahsil office shows that the suit plot No. 931 was never recorded in the name of any person in the recent survey conducted by the government and any person did not make claim at the time of survey; that nobody had paid rent against the said suit plot No. 931 and the plaintiff at the time of survey did not produce any documents or deeds before the concerned surveyor. As per law there was no claim against the suit plot. The suit plot has been duly recorded in the name of government as khas khatian No. 1. The defendants as such have prayed for dismissal of the suit.

5. The plaintiff and defendants adduced witnesses before the learned trial Court and all the witnesses were cross-examined by the parties.

6. The trial Court on considering the facts and circumstances of the case as well as the relevant provision of law dismissed the suit.

7. The plaintiff against the judgment and decree passed by the Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar Brahmanbaria preferred Title Appeal No. 61 of 2006 before the learned District Judge and the learned District Judge considering the facts and circumstances of the case as well as the evidence on record allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar in Title suit No. 110 of 2005.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge in Title Appeal No. 61 of 2006 the respondent petitioner preferred this revision before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

9. Mrs. Salma Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney General for the petitioner submits that the appellate Court without considering the documents in record and the evidence by the parties allowed the appeal resulting in an error in decision occasioning failure of justice; that the learned Assistant Judge being the trial Court of the suit came to the finding that the plaintiff has failed to prove that the settlement plot No. 931/3 and SA plot No. 931 are the same and also came to finding that the plaintiff did not file SA khatian No. 111 and, as such, the learned Assistant Judge rightly dismissed the suit. She further submits that appellate Court came to a wrong finding about the title of plaintiff relying on mutation khatian and rent receipt over the suit land. As per law the mutation khatian and rent receipts are not the documents of title. The learned appellate Court failed to consider this vital aspect of law and, as such, committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree are liable to be set aside.

10. Mrs Rezina Mahmud, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party on the other hand submits that the defendants petitioners have no prima facie title and possession in the suit land; that the plaintiff opposite party have title and possession in the suit land; that the learned Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar failed to consider facts, circumstances and evidence on record and dismissed the suit. She further submits that the learned District Judge, considering the facts, circumstances and evidence on record allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge and, as such, there is no scope to interfere in the impugned judgment and decree of the learned District Judge.

11. The learned Advocate cited the decision in the case of Abul Hossain vs Amjad Hossain reported in 62 DLR (AD) 436 in support of her contention.

12. Now, the point for determination is whether the Court below committed any illegality or material irregularity in passing his decision which is occasioning any failure of justice.

13. There is no denying of the fact that Bishnu Kapali was the original owner of the suit jote and he died leaving behind a son Nagarbashi Kapali and a daughter Ananta Bala who became the successors of Bishnu Kapali. The contention of the plaintiff is that after the death of Bishnu Kapali, Nagarbashi Kapali and his sister Ananta Bala sold the suit property by two registered deeds dated 22-12-1952 AD to Moezuddin @ Darag Ali, the father of the plaintiff, and Mongal Miah the paternal uncle of the plaintiff. Mondal Miah had no issue and thus Moezuddin @ Darag Ali became owner of the entire suit property. The SA khatian of the suit property was rightly recorded in the name of Darag Ali @ Moezuddin the father of the plaintiff. The plaintiff got some of the suit land mutated in his name in SA khatian. He paid rent of the suit property including other properties till 2001 to the government. The suit property was wrongly recorded in the field khatian in the name of the government during last settlement survey.

14. On the other hand, the case of the government is that the registered deeds of the plaintiff were fake and fraudulent. The suit property was rightly recorded in the name of defendants during last settlement survey. It is further stated that SA record was prepared in the name of Mahananda Kapali, son of Govinda Kapali in khatian No. 111. An area of 70 decimals land had been recorded in the name of Darag Ali in khatian No. 13 and another and 57 decimals had been recorded in the name of other's. It is also stated that record of Tahsil office shows that the suit plot No. 931 was never recorded in the name of any person in the recent survey conducted by the government and any person did not claim at the time of survey. Nobody had paid rent against the said suit plot No. 931. The plaintiff at the time of survey did not produce any documents or deeds before the concerned surveyor. As per law, there was no claim against the suit plot and thus, the suit plot has been duly recorded in the name of government as khas khatian No. 1.

15. It is consistent view of our apex Court that plaintiff is to prove his case and he cannot get a decree on the weakness or failure of the defendant. The plaintiff is to prove his own case even in a ex parte proceeding. Disbelieve of the defence case 'ipso facto' does not make the plaintiff's case believable. Even in the case of an ex parte disposal of a suit, the Court is required to come to a finding on the assessment of the materials on record that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case. I find support of the above view in the case of Khandaker Mobarak Ali vs Jahanara Begum reported in 1 ADC (2004) 401 and Jinnatunnessa vs Bangladesh 48 DLR 208.

16. Now let us see whether the plaintiff opposite party has succeeded in proving his case. The plaintiff opposite party has brought this suit claiming for declaration of title in the suit property as filed khatian has been wrongly recorded in the name of the government.

17. The plaintiff have examined three PWs and adduced evidence supporting the title and possession of the plaintiff and the plaintiff also filed certified copies of the CR khatian No.47 marked exhibit (1), original document dated 22-12-1951 marked exhibit-2 and original documents being No. 8774 marked exhibit-3 and certified copies of RoR khatian No. 13 marked exhibit 4, Mutation khatian No. 323 marked exhibit 5 and some Dakhilas marked exhibits to 6(1) to 6 (Tha) in support of his title and possession.

18. Admittedly Bishnu Kapali was the original owner of the suit property and admittedly he died leaving behind two heirs namely a son Nagarbashi Kapali and a daughter Ananta Bala who sold the suit property by two registered deeds dated 22-12-1952 vide exhibit 2 and 3 respectively to the predecessors of the plaintiff appellant. The government though challenged the two registered deeds more than 30 years back yet could not succeed to show any evidence in the slightest form that the documents (exhibit-2 and 3 were false and fraudulent). Mere contention of a party is not enough at all to treat a registered deed as fraudulent or false.

19. The learned Assistant Attorney General for the petitioner government could not succeed to show any legal interpretation that the deeds (exhibit 2 and 3 of the plaintiff appellant were fraudulent for such and such grounds. So in a nutshell, it can be said that the plaintiff appellant petitioner Abdul Aziz has bona fide right, title and interest of the suit land.

20. Moreover, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner referring sub section 1 of the section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act submits that the procedure for extinguishment of interest of raiyats in certain cases in section 92 of the SAT Act which runs thus:

92. Extinguishment of Interest of Raiyats in certain cases—(1) The interest of a raiyat in a holding shall be ex tongued—

(a) When he dies intestate leaving no heir enlitlea to inherit under the law of inheritance to which he is subject;

(b) When he surrenders his holding at the end of any agricultural year by giving notice in the prescribed form and in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period to the revenue officer;

(c) When he voluntarily abandons his residence without making any arrangement for payment of the rent as it falls due and ceases to cultivate his holding either by himself or by members of his family or by or with the aid of servants or labourer with the aid of partners or bargadars for a period of three successive years, or

(d) When such interest had devolved by inheritance under the law of inheritance to which such raiyat is subject on a person who is not a bona fide cultivator and such person has not cultivated the land comprised in the holding either by himself or by members of his family or by or with the aid of, servants or labourers or with the aid of partners or bargadars during the period of five years from the date on which such interest has so devolved on him and there is no sufficient cause why he has not so cultivated the land.

21. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that none of the conditions stated in the above section fall in the instant case.

22. She further refers sub-section 3 of the section 92 of the SAT Act which runs thus:

"(3) Before entering on a holding under subsection (2)' the Revenue Officer shall cause a notice to be published in the prescribed manner declaring his intention to so enter on the holding and specifying the reasons thereof and also inviting objections from all persons interested in the holding and shall consider any objection that may be submitted to him within the period specified in that behalf in the notice and shall record a decision."

<u>23. Referring subsection 3 she further submits that before entering on a holding under subsection (2), the Revenue Officer did not comply with the procedure of taking of holding in the name of the government and did not specify the reasons thereof.</u>

<u>24. I find substance in the arguments of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party and I am of the view that there is no ground of taking of the suit holding in the custody of the government and no legal procedure was followed and, as such, taking over of the holding is illegal.</u>

25. In this respect the learned Advocate for the opposite parties cited the decision in case of Hridoy Ranjan Day vs Niranjan Dey reported in 6 MLR (AD) 267 = 54 DLR (AD) 16 wherein it has been held that person entering into possession of land on the basis of defective title document and having been in continuous possession thereof for more than 12 years acquires title preferred by adverse possession as contemplated under section 28 of the Limination Act, 1908 and, as such, he is entitled to get decree for declaration of his title.

26. I may profitably refer the decision in the case of Abul Hossain vs Amjad Hossain reported in 62 DLR (AD) 436 and provision of section 10 of the Evidence Act which provide for a presumption of ownership in favour of the person who is in possession of the property. A person in possession of land however, imperfect his title may be, has a good title against the whole world except the true owner and until the true owner comes in Court to assert a claim to the property. Possession is evidence of title and gives a good title as against wrong doer.

<u>27. In the instant case since the plaintiff opposite party have been in possession on the basis of deeds, rent receipt and filed record which are though defective title still they have acquired title on the basis of continuous possession in the suit land for more than 12 years. A person remains in possession of the land on the basis of defective title for more than 12 years can acquire title. A person in possession of the land can only be dispossessed by another having better title.</u>

28. The scope of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is now well settled. Consistent pronouncements by the Highest Court of the country have made it abundantly clear that a Court of revision under section 115(1) CPC can interfere with the findings of fact as the final Court of facts only in exceptional circumstances when the findings are shockingly perverse or these are vitiated by non reading and misreading of the material evidence or misconstruction of any important documents affecting the merit of the suit. The learned Advocate for the defendants petitioners have not been able to find out any such legal infirmity in the impugned judgment which calls for any interference.

29. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, I am of the view that the learned Court of appeal below on proper consideration of the evidence on record and after adverting to the reasons assigned by the trial Court reversed the judgment passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Nasir Nagar. The findings recorded by the learned Court of appeal below are well supported by the evidence on record and are based on correct principle of the appreciation of the evidence. I find no illegality in the impugned judgment to call for any interference by this Court exercising revisional power.

30. In the result the revision fails and the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

Kamal-ul-Alam, Advocate--For Opposite Party No. 5.

parties:
Fairdeal Marine Services ------ Petitioner
VS
MV Peleas K ------ Opposite-Parties.
full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed J: This Execution Case arises out of Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999 that was filed on 21-3-1999 for recovery of the outstanding payment of a bunker bill for an amount of Taka 19,70,000, including interest and costs, and pertaining to the vessel 'MV Peleas K'. In decreeing the Suit for an amount of Taka 19,70,000 in favour of the plaintiff and against the principal-defendants, the Court ordered on the Plaintiffs entitlement to recover the decrial amount by encashment of the Bank Guarantee bearing No. 864 /CG9900107 dated 24-3-1999 issued by the Standard Chartered Bank, 20 Motijheel, C/A, Dhaka. There has also been an order in Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999 on the entitlement of the Plaintiff to interest on the decretal amount at the rate of 8% per annum from the date of institution of the Suit till the date of realisation of that amount. The plaintiff-decree-holder-petitioner (hereinafter referred to as the petitioner') having filed this Execution Case on 10-3-2005, this Court in its order dated 9-5-2005 noted that the said interest amount as computed till the date of filing of the Execution Case amounted to Taka 11,33,562.50 thereby, leading to the total claim to amount to Taka 31,03,562.50. The Bank Guarantee having, by that date been already encashed pursuant to a previous order of the Court dated 1-3-2005 and consequentially the amount of Taka 19,70,000 found lying in the account of the Marshal of the Admiralty Court, the Court in disposing of the case accordingly directed the Marshal of the Court to take necessary steps to make payment of Taka 19,70,000 then remaining deposited in the account of the Marshal of the Court. It is noted that the Marshal upon obtaining permission from the Bangladesh Bank remitted Taka 19,70,000.00 to the petitioner's account on 21-9-2005 leaving an unpaid balance amount to Taka 11,33,562.50. That led to the application dated 25-9-2005 being filed by the petitioner for a direction upon the defendant No. 5 judgment-debtor-opposite party No. 5 (hereinafter referred to as the 'opposite party No. 5') to pay the balance decretal amount of Taka 11,33,562.50. In the application the petitioner contends that since the decree has been passed against the defendant Nos. 1 to 5 in the Suit, the petitioner is, therefore, entitled to recover the balance of the decretal amount of Taka 11,33,562.50 from the properties of the opposite party No. 5 who is the agent of the vessel 'MV Peleas This application appears to have been necessitated upon the failure of the opposite party No. 5 agent in coming forward to pay the balance decretal amount in spite of the receipt of the summons of this Court in connection with the Execution Case. The prayer in the application is for the issuance of a show cause notice upon. the opposite party No. 5 as to why it shall not be directed to pay the said balance decretal amount within a specified period, and why in the event of failing to do so the said amount shall not be recovered from the sale proceeds of the properties of the opposite party No. 5 specified in Schedule-'A' to the Application. It is noted that in allowing the said application this Court by its Order dated 15-11-2005 ordered for the issuance of such notice and further directed the properties mentioned in Schedule 'A' to the Application to be attached pending hearing of the show cause notice. This elicited a response from the opposite party No. 5 in the manner of an Affidavit-in-Opposition in which the opposite party No. 5 has raised certain grounds, primarily as to the nullity in the eye of law of the Judgment and Decree passed in Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999 in terms of operation of the same against the opposite party No. 5. The opposite party No. 5 submits that having regard to the facts and given that there was no contract between the opposite party No. 5 and the petitioner for the supply of the bunkers to the vessel, having further regard to the fact that the opposite party No. 1 was the disclosed principal of the agent opposite party No. 5 and the same was known to the petitioner, the opposite party No. 5 cannot, therefore, be held liable for the alleged breach of contract by the principal defendant-judgment-debtor-opposite party No. 1 according to the provisions of section 230 of the Contract Act, 1872. The opposite party No. 5 also maintains that having regard to the fact that the opposite party. No. 5 was not the agent of the opposite party No. 1 vessel when the cause of action for filing Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999 arose in December 1998 when the petitioner supplied bunkers to the opposite party No. 1 vessel at a port in Fujairah, UAE, and having regard further to the fact that the opposite party No. 5 became the agent of the opposite party No. 1 vessel in Bangladesh in February, 1999 when the opposite party No. 1 vessel arrived at Chittagong, the opposite party No. 5 cannot, therefore, be made liable in law for the claim against its principal the opposite party No. 1 vessel for the cause of action which arose long before the opposite party No. 5 became the agent of the opposite party No. 1 vessel. Consequently, it is the contention of the opposite party No. 5 that since the Judgment and Decree passed against it in Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999 must be considered a nullity in the eye of law and, as such, not executable against the opposite party No. 5, the said application dated 25-9-2005 for the execution of the said Decree against the opposite party No. 5 must also be held to be not maintainable.

2. The Affidavit-in-Opposition is also in evidence of the contention of the opposite party No. 5 that the said execution application dated 25-9-2005 is not maintainable against the opposite party No. 5 given the admitted fact that the petitioner in its original application dated 10-3-2005 for execution of the Decree under Order XXI, rule 11(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 ("the Code") having not made any prayer in the relevant Form No. (J) 47 for execution of the Decree against the opposite party No. 5 and indeed, having not spelt out that the mode of such execution would be by sale of the properties of the opposite party No. 5 or otherwise and, thereby, having not complied with the requirements of the relevant provisions of Order XXI, rule 11(2) of the Code, the said application dated 10-3-2005 is not in accordance with law and, consequently, is not maintainable against opposite party No. 5 and liable to be rejected under the provisions of Order XXI, rule 17 of the Code. On that premise, the application dated 29-9-2005 is also submitted to be not maintainable and, therefore, liable to be rejected.

3. Heard the learned Advocates for the petitioner and the opposite parties, perused the various applications, including the application for direction, and the Affidavit-in-Opposition on behalf of the opposite party No. 5.

4. The learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Sk Siddique has at the outset pointed out to this Court that Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999 is one in rem against all named defendants as also otherwise interested in the vessel. The Suit falls under section 5 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, the relevant portion of which reads thus:

"The High Court of Admiralty shall have jurisdiction over any claim for necessaries supplied to any ship elsewhere than in the port to which the ship belongs.

5. Mr Siddique submits that a suit in rem cannot commence unless the vessel and the owner is represented in Court by a local agent and that under section 5 of the Act of 1861 the very presence of an agent is necessary for this Court to assume jurisdiction over a case. It is submitted that the vessel 'MV Peleas K' called at Chittagong Port under the agency of the opposite party No. 5 who gave a declaration under section 55(d) and section 78 of the Customs Act, 1969 and that, as such, upon the admission of Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999, the vessel 'MV Peleas K' was arrested by an Order of this Court on 21-3-1999. It is submitted that, consequentially, the opposite party No. 5 received the writs of arrest on behalf of all the defendants. It is submitted that apparent from the Orders of this Court dated 16-3-2003, 16-3-2004, 19-5-2004 and 18-5-2004 is the fact that notwithstanding the said vessel being within this Court's jurisdiction and as formally represented by the opposite party No. 5, the said party as defendant No. 5 never appeared in the Suit nor in these execution proceedings till after receipt of this Court's Order dated 15- 11-2005. It is submitted that given these circumstances it would not be open to this Executing Court at this juncture to consider the above grounds raised by the opposite party No. 5 against the execution of the Decree. Given that these defences and grounds could have been agitated by the opposite party No. 5 at the time of the hearing of the suit and, thereby, at that more appropriate stage giving this Court an opportunity to consider the same upon going through any oral and documentary evidence as may have been adduced and produced by the opposite party No. 5 as a named defendant and, in turn, providing the plaintiff an opportunity to cross-examine the opposite party No. 5, Mr Siddique points out that upon a perusal of the affidavit-in-opposition a fine distinction needs now to be drawn between (a) a decree passed without jurisdiction, and (b) a decree that is a nullity, but only against the opposite party No. 5. He submits in this regard that if this Executing Court finds the Suit to be maintainable under section 5 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 it would thereafter be difficult for it to go the extra length to examine the extent to which the decree is nevertheless a nullity against the opposite party No, 5 as that would require a consideration of the case on its merits which this Court cannot readily do. In this regard, Mr Siddique has referred to the judgment in Ramjan Khan vs Obaidul Huq Chowdhury reported in 28 DLR (AD) 57 for the authority that the power of the executing Court to test the validity of a decree is limited to seeing whether the decree was passed without jurisdiction or is a nullity, or there exists some other exceptional ground as to the excitability of a decree.

6. The learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 5 Mr Kamal-ul Alam has also submitted on the jurisdiction of an executing Court as operates, albeit exceptionally and within extremely narrow limits, to go behind a decree in questioning its legality or correctness. That exception is well explained, for example in Sunder Dass vs Ram Parkash reported in AIR 1977 (SC) 1201, at paragraph 3, page 1205 thus:

"Now, the law is well settled that an executing Court cannot go behind the decree nor can it question its legality or correctness. But there is one exception to this general rule and that is, that where the decree sought to be executed is a nullity for lack of inherent jurisdiction in the Court passing it, its invalidity can be set up in an execution proceeding. Where there is lack of inherent jurisdiction, it goes to the root of the competence of the Court to try the case and a decree which is a nullity is void and can be declared to he void by any Court in which it is presented. Its nullity can be set up whenever it is sought to be enforced or relied upon and even at the stage of execution or even in collateral proceedings. The executing Court can, therefore, entertain an objection that the decree is a nullity and can refuse to execute the decree. By doing so, the executing Court would not incur the reproach that it is going behind the decree, because the decree being null and void, there would really be no decree at all. Vide Kiran Singh vs Chaman Paswan, (1955) 1 SCR 117 = (AIR 1954 SC 340) and Hiralal Patni vs Kali Nath, (1962) 2 SCR 747 = (AIR 1962 SC 199),"

Further, reference is had of Md Ahsanullah vs Arafatunnessa reported in 33 DLR (AD) 17, at paragraph 4, page 20 thus:

"At the outset, it is to be observed that the jurisdiction of the executing Court to go behind the decree is now well settled and the locus classic us on this point is the case of Gorachand Haider vs Prafulla Kumar Roy, a Full Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in 29 CWN 948, which has been uniformly followed since then. The proposition set out there is, that where the decree presented for execution was made by a Court which apparently had no jurisdiction whether pecuniary or territorial or in respect of the judgment debtor's person to make the decree, the executing Court is entitled to refuse to execute it on the ground that it was made without jurisdiction. It was further held that within these narrow limits the executing Court is authorised to question the validity of the decree."

7. M Alam has at considerable length argued on those facts of this case bearing upon the date of occurrence of non-payment, the date thereafter that the opposite party No. 5 became a Declaring Agent of the opposite party No. 1 vessel when it arrived at Chittagong Port, the absence of any allegation of any cause of action against the opposite party No. 5 and indeed of any contractual or personal liability of the opposite party No. 5, to substantiate his submissions generally that the Decree is without jurisdiction as there was no cause of action against the opposite party No. 5. He has also at length submitted on section 230 of the Contract Act, 1872 which provides that an agent cannot personally enforce nor be bound by contracts on behalf of the principal in the absence of a contract to that effect. The thrust of Mr Siddique's argument in response has been that all these facts and issues have to be deemed subsumed under the broader question of whether the Decree passed in Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999 is within the jurisdiction vested in the Admiralty Court under section 5 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 or not.

<u>8. On a clear reading of section 5 of the Act of 1861 this Court is of the view that the judgment passed in decreeing the said Admiralty Suit against the defendants ex parte cannot be said to have been passed without jurisdiction. In that regard, this Court finds itself to be in agreement with Mr Siddique's submission that the Admiralty Court having assumed jurisdiction under section 5 of the Act of 1861 to consider the claim of the plaintiff for supply of bunkers to the vessel 'MV Peleas K', section 230 of the Contract Act, 1872 cannot be said to have an application in these facts and cannot, therefore, he interpreted to have a coextensive application with section 5 of the Act of 1861 for assumption of jurisdiction for passing a decree for claims arising from the supply of fuel to the vessel. In this regard, Mr Siddique appears to suggest that the jurisdiction exercised under section 5 of the Act of 1861 operates with a certain sense of exclusivity and in precedence to the laws and authorities relied upon by Mr Alam in questioning the jurisdiction exercised in Admiralty Suit No. 37 of 1999. This Court is inclined to accept that submission made by Mr Siddique and finds that proceeding under section 5 of the Act, 1861 the Admiralty Court, and given the non-appearance by the opposite party No. 5 at all stages in the Suit and the Admiralty Court not, therefore, being put on notice of issues and evidence that are only now being raised in this Execution Case by the opposite party No. 5 for the first time in its Affidavit-in-Opposition, duly and aptly exercised its jurisdiction culminating in the Judgment and Decree of 9-8-2004. By that reason the necessity of this Court to discuss at length the merits or demerits of the submissions made and response thereto regarding, for example, the application of section 230 of the Contract Act, 1872 and sections 55(d) and 78 of the Customs Act, 1969 is obviated or made unnecessary.</u>

9. This, therefore, brings this Court to deal with the second issue involved concerning the initiation of these execution proceedings under Order XXI, rule 11(2) of the Code. In this regard, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 5 Mr Alam, in recounting the execution process, throws light on that which he terms as the First Execution Case No. 2 of 2005 as evident in the decree being satisfied on payment of the principal decretal amount of Taka 19,70,000 by the Marshal of this Court to the petitioner. Mr Alam submits further that the First Execution Order' of 9-5-2005 being lawfully satisfied by the encashment of the earlier referred Bank Guarantee, there was, however, no modality described in that Order that would satisfy payment of the interest amount. It is at the juncture thus, Mr Alam submits, that complexities arose as evident in the filing on 25-9-2005 of a second application, i.e., the application for direction upon the opposite party No. 5 to pay the balance decretal amount of Taka 11,33,562.50 and for attachment of the property of the opposite party No. 5, when in law the proper course to have been adopted by the petitioner would have been the filing of an extension case for a possible recovery of the said interest amount. Contending in this context that the piecemeal execution of a decree, firstly for the principal amount and subsequently for the amount of interest, is not permissible in law by reason of being in contravention of Order XXI, rule 11(2)(g) of the Code. Mr Alam has referred to Panaji vs Ratanchand reported in AIR 1933 (Bombay), 364 for the authority that execution in different stages or by piecemeal fashion is not permitted under the law. In the Panaji Case, the Bombay Court dealt with similar facts and circumstances where a decree executed earlier for principal and costs was held to operate as a bar for a subsequent application for the balance interest amount. Mr Alam submits that the operating rule in this regard, is formulated thus in the Panaji Case at pages 365 and 366:

"Under English law, it is not permissible to levy execution of a money decree in different stages. It has been held that where there is only one judgment for a sum of money there can only be one execution upon it if piecemeal execution is permissible it seems that the party executing must show, not that right is forbidden by the Code, but that it is conferred by the Code. There is nothing in the Code which expressly authorises piecemeal execution, and a good many of the provisions of Order XXI, which deal with execution, seems opposed to the idea that there can be more than one execution of a money decree. For example, rule 10, Order XXI provides for the execution of the decree, and not of a portion of the decree. Rule 11(2)(g) provides that in the particulars to be stated in the application for execution the amount, with interest if any due upon the decree, must be stated, and there is no express provision for stating the amount for which the execution creditor desires to levy execution."

10. Further, in so explaining the law and procedure, Beaumont, CJ opined thus in the Panaji Case at 366:

"In my opinion, there is no authority for the provision that a single money decree for sums immediately payable at the date of execution can be executed at different times. I think that the correct rule, and certainly the rule of convenience, is that a party having a right to execute a decree for money presently payable must enforce the whole decree at the same time."

11. The consequences of any attempt at a piecemeal execution has been split out thus in Ramdas Mukhopadhay vs Liday Chand reported in AIR 1949 Calcutta, 228 at paragraph 6 229:

"The next question which has been urged is that the decree-holder cannot at his option break up the liability without the consent of the judgment-debtors. There is nothing in law to prevent a decree-holder from giving up part of his claim and executing his decree only for a portion. He certainly cannot split up his claim and ask for separate execution proceedings to be started in regard to each particular portion of the claim. But there is nothing to prevent him from starting execution proceedings with regard to part of the claim provided that he does not proceed with the other part. Subsequently, he is not allowed in law to proceed with the part which was not proceeded with before."

12. Mr Alam has in this regard pointed out that the first execution petition dated 10-3-2005, and as initiated this Execution Case with the filing of the Form Na. (j) 47 under Order XXI, rule 11 of the Code, suffers from certain fatal flaws. Thus, it appears that the decree-holder has not identified in Column 9 of the Form either the defendant No. 5 opposite party No. 5 as a person against whom execution is sought or taken care to specify therein the particulars of the properties of the opposite party No. 5 as are now sought to be sold upon attachment. This, it is submitted, constitutes non-compliance with the requirements of Order XXI, rule 11(2)(i) and (j). In that regard, it is brought to the attention of this Court that there is nothing in the said Form as states that the relief sought for is by attachment or sale of anybody's property, let alone that of the opposite party No. 5. It is noted in this regard that Column 10 of the Form captioned "Relief prayed" has been left completely blank. It is also submitted that beyond specifying in Column 11 of the Form the fact and mode of executing the Decree for the principal decretal amount of Taka 19,70,000 out of the Bank Guarantee amount lying in the account of the Marshal of the Court no other mode in which the assistance of this Court is required is specified for realisation of the interest amount of Taka 11,33,562.50. In conjunction with this Mr Alam has cited Satish Chandra Mookerjee vs Puma Chandra Dutt reported in 11 Indian Cases (1911) 696 as authority for the view that an application for execution of a decree, which does not specify the mode in which the assistance of the Court is required, is defective, and unless the defect is remedied, the application must be dismissed. Mr Alam submits that such deficiencies in this case cumulatively operate to make the execution proceedings as not being maintainable and, therefore, laible to be rejected against the opposite party No. 5. In this regard, he has further referred, in particular, to the Civil Rules and Orders and drawn this Court's attention to the provisions of Rule 170 as prescribe that amongst the particulars to be compulsorily specified in an application for execution under Order XXI, rule 11(2) shall be those as go towards constituting the "whole of the relief' and that in that regard "interest" should be "correctly calculated and the total amount for which execution is prayed should be entered in column 11 of Form No. (J) 47." This Court notes that the Rule further enjoins that the "Court shall not grant any relief not claimed by the execution petition, but should insist on the applicant setting out accurately the reliefs which he does claim."

13. Mr Siddique has generally submitted in response that the relevant Form No. J (47) is to be read as having provided the details of the Decree including the interest amount and that, therefore, there is no further requirement to specify each and every item in such Form. Drawing this Court's attention to Order XXI, rule 11(1), Mr Siddique submits further that as the Decree is a money decree there is indeed, no necessity to comply with Order XXI, rule 2, and that in such a case this Court could have had, even on an oral application of the decree-holder at the time of the passing of the decree, ordered immediate execution thereof. This argument, in the view of this Court, appears specious given that the Decree-Holder-petitioner evidently chose not to pursue an execution by oral application but rather opted to apply for the execution of a decree in writing, thereby, in the view of this Court, attracting and submitting to the specific provisions and requirements of Order XXI, rule 11(2).

14. Evidently admitting that the relevant Form No. J (47) is deficient in certain aspects, Mr Siddique has, however, submitted that every omission in an application for execution is not necessarily to be deemed a material irregularity as would vitiate the execution proceedings. He submits by reference to Saudamini vs Jessore Regd. Loan Co. reported in AIR 1926 (Cal) 1146 that whether an omission is or is not material will depend on the facts of each particular case. The test is possibly also of deciding whether an application under Order XXI, rule 11(2), though not conforming strictly to legal requirements and prescriptions, can be said nevertheless to contain all material particulars required for the purpose of execution (Central Exchange Bank Ltd vs Ch. Dilawar Ali Khan reported in PLD 1965 (WP) (Lahore) 628 and the ratio in Abdul Salam Sahib vs Batehu Veerabhadraraju reported in AIR 1928 (Madras) 129 (2) appears to the effect that relief granted by overlooking "certain small informalities" may not be challenged. Applying that test and ratio the absence in Column 11 of any description or particulars of the property of the opposite party No. 5 sought to be attached and indeed, that of any mention of any relief sought by attachment or sale of the properties of the opposite party No. 5 in the said Column of Form No. J (47) are now submitted by Mr Siddique, and in terms of non-compliance with the requirements of Order XXI, rule 11(2)(j), as not constituting illegalities but mere irregularities. Mr Siddique has referred to Kanmal Meghraj vs Govind Prasad reported in AIR 1946 Nagpur 365 in arguing that if the facts permit then an executing Court can, on the particulars furnished, proceed to do all that is necessary for the decree-holder. Reference has also been had of Nathmal vs Balkrishna reported in AIR 1941 (Nagpur), 152 where it was held that since Order XXI, rule 11(2)(j) speaks nothing of the specification of the property, all that the decree-holder is required to set forth is the mode in which he seeks the assistance of the Court. Mr Siddique cites the Nathmal Case as authority also for the view that the mode will be considered to be sufficiently indicated, for example, by a statement of attachment being sought of certain property even without specifying the particulars of the same.

Upon an examination of the Form No. J (47) in this case, this Court finds that the cases as above referred are distinguishable from the one at hand as Column 11 in describing the "mode in which the assistance of the Court is required" states simply.

"The Marshal of the Court may kindly be directed to pay to the Fairdeal Marine Services. Fujairah. USDS A/C NR 7-418080-840-243, National Bank of Ras Al Khaimah, Kalba Branch, Kalba, United Arab Emirates (UAE). Correspondent Bank, Bank of New York, New York (USA). A/C NR: 890-0056-630 of National Bank of Ras Al Khaimah decree holder an amount of Taka 19,70,000 (Nineteen lac seventy thousand) only now lying in account of the Marshal of this Court."

15. On the basis of the above this Court finds a total absence of any indication of the fact of attachment of any property per se belonging to whomsoever as could reasonably be said to now assist this Court to proceed to do what is claimed to be necessary for the decree-holder-petitioner in the facts and circumstances. This was the state of affairs before this Court on the date that the initial execution order was made on 9-5-2005 and this Court, though taking note of the claimed decretal amount of Taka 19,70,000.00 plus interest of Taka 11,33,562.50, ordered simply the making of the payment of the former amount and no more. On a query by this Court, Mr Siddique submits that this Court at the time could not order a payment of the interest amount as admittedly the Decree-Holder-petitioner did not have the relevant information as to how and from whom that interest amount was to be satisfied and claimed. This Court has also having taken note of the observation in that Order of 9-5-2005 that there was no appearance by any party on that date before this Court in this matter. However, Mr Siddique states that he was, in fact, present in Court on that particular date. Be that as it may, the circumstances in this case thereafter gave rise to the application dated 25-9-2005 for a direction upon the opposite party No. 5 to pay the balance decretal amount leading to the Order dated 15-11-2005, as more immediately concerns this Court now.

16. Upon a due consideration of all the facts and circumstances of this case this Court has arrived at the conclusion that the Admiralty Court having duly and properly exercised its jurisdiction under section 5 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, there remains no justification for this Court to go behind the Judgment and Decree dated 9-8-2004 to probe into questions of. fact and law raised by the opposite party No. 5 in its Affidavit-in-Opposition seeking this Court's declaration as to the nullity of such Judgment and Decree vis-a-vis the opposite party No. 5. That being the case, this Court finds, nevertheless, that it has jurisdiction to inquire into the sufficiency of the procedure adopted by the decree-holder-petitioner in executing the Decree. In that regard, this Court finds the information provided in the Form No. J (47) to be deficient and wholly inappropriate of the execution of the decree beyond the principal decretal amount of Taka 19,70,000 as was indeed effected by this Court's Order dated 9-5-2005. Beyond that this Court finds no other information, particularly in Column No. 11 of Form No. J (47) as would assist this Court in any way to secure to the decree-holder-petitioner the payment of the interest amount of Taka 11,33,562.50 upto the date of the filing of this Execution Case. By filing the application dated 25-9-2005 the petitioner has in effect sought a piecemeal execution of the decree, firstly, for the principal amount and subsequently for the amount of interest that is contrary to the express provisions of Order XXI, rule 11(2)(g). The decree-holder-petitioner had a right to seek a comprehensive and complete relief the first time around, but having not done so, as is evident in the facts and circumstances of this case, shall not, therefore, have any avenue open to it for placing claims periodically at subsequent dates. Having thus failed to so fully exercise its right by execution of the entire decree at one go the decree-holder-petitioner, and as is evident in the execution petition of 10-3-2005, having asked this Court to enforce the decree for the sum only of Taka 19,70,000, a sum lesser than the gross claimed amount of Taka 31,03,562.50 inclusive of interest, must now be taken to have accordingly waived the right to claim the balance amount of Taka 11,33,562.50. Requiring this Court to now allow satisfaction of the claim to the balance interest amount in the manner as sought in the application dated 25-9-2005 is tantamount to effectively asking this Court to innovate on the execution application and case which this Court is now reluctant to undertake in the facts and circumstances.

In light of the above, this Court finds no merit in the application dated 25-9-2005 for direction upon the opposite party No. 5 to pay the balance decretal amount of Taka 11,33,562.50. Accordingly, that application is dismissed. The ad interim order of attachment dated 15-11-2005 pertaining to the properties of the opposite party No. 5 and as mentioned and specified in Schedule 'A' to the application is hereby necessarily recalled and vacated.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka dismissing the revisional application by the petitioners and affirming the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the Assistant judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka allowing the application of the defendants under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside the judgment and ex parte decree dated 23-6-99 and restoring the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 in its original file and number should not be set aside.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 215 of 1996 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka subsequently transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Nawabganj and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession against the defendant-opposite parties stating, inter alia, that the suit property being homestead property belong to Hanif Sarker, who transferred the same by a registered sale deed dated 12-2-1964 in favour of the mother of the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 1-2. The defendant Nos. 1-2 were allowed to live in the said homestead as licensee or with permission. The mother of the plaintiffs gifted the suit property and delivered the possession of the same to the plaintiffs by an oral gift dated 17-9-92. The defendant Nos. 1-2 obtained permission from the plaintiffs to live therein as licensee as before. Thereafter the mother of the plaintiffs swore an affidavit before the Notary Public, Dhaka in respect of her earlier oral gift in favour of the plaintiffs. That other two brothers namely, Kabir and Humayun of the plaintiffs were the witness in the said affidavit and the plaintiffs are in possession of some portion of the suit land through their tenant. That the plaintiffs served a notice upon the defendants to vacate the suit premises but the defendants declined to do so, hence the instant suit.

3. The summons of the suit were duly served upon the defendants but they failed to appear before the Court as a result the suit was decreed by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka ex parte by his judgment and decree dated 23-6-99.

4. The defendant-opposite party No. 2 Md Mizanur Rahman filed on application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the aforesaid ex parte decree and the above application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 35 of 1999 and at the same time he preferred a Title Appeal being No. 769 of 1989 before the District Judge, Dhaka against the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka.

5. Thereafter, the aforesaid Title Appeal No. 769 of 1999 was allowed by the District Judge by his judgment and decree dated 29-3-2001 by setting aside the District Judge by his judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka and sent back the suit on remand for further hearing.

6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 29-3-2001 passed in Title Appeal No. 769 of 1999 the plaintiff-petitioners preferred a Civil Revision No. 3834 of 2001 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule and ultimately the High Court Division was pleased to make the Rule absolute by their judgment and decree dated 8-1-2002 and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court (District Judge).

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 8-1-2002 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3834 of 2001 the defendant-opposite party No. 2 preferred another Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002 before the Appellate Division, Supreme Court of Bangladesh and after hearing their Lordships were pleased to dismiss the aforesaid Leave Petition by their judgment and order dated 18-1-2003.

8. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 and another filed an application in Civil Revision No. 3834 of 2001 for vacating and re-calling the judgment and order dated 28-1-2002 and after hearing the High Court Division was pleased to reject the same on 5-3-2003 and against the said judgment and order dated 28-1-2002 the defendant-opposite party No. 1 and another preferred a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1053 of 2003 before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and the same was also dismissed on 8-8-2004.

9. In the meantime, defendant-opposite party No.1 filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial Court on 20-2-2000 and the same was rejected as Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 for setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka. On the other hand, the plaintiff-petitioners filed a Title Execution Case No. 4 of 2000 before the Court of Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka.

10. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 appeared in the aforesaid execution case and filed an application for stay of all further proceedings of the Title Execution Case No. 4 of 2000 till disposal of the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 and the plaintiff-petitioners-filed a written objection against the said application for stay and after hearing the Executing Court was pleased to reject the same on 30-10-2003 and the defendant-opposite party No. 1 was evicted from the suit land and possession of the property was handed over to the plaintiff-petitioners on 30-11-2003 at 2-30 PM through bailiff.

11. The defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 threatened the plaintiff-petitioner No. 3 and compelled her to file different applications on 20-3-2005 and give deposition before the trial Court for allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 for setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 passed by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka and in order to save her life she did the same which was not done voluntarily but under the threat and coercion of defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 which did not carry any value in the eye of law.

12. That the above Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 was heard on 23-3-2005 and the trial Court was pleased to allow the same by his judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 and restored the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 to its original file and number after setting aside the ex parte decree dated 23-6-99.

13. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka allowing the case setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 the plaintiff-petitioners preferred a Civil Prevision No. 262 of 2005 before the District Judge, Dhaka.

14. In the said Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 the plaintiff-petitioners and defendant-opposite party No. 1 filed a solenama supported by an affidavits sworn by the plaintiff-petitioner No. 3 and defendant-opposite party No. 1 before the Affidavit Commissioner of the Court of District Judge, Dhaka on 4-10-2005 in presence of their learned Advocates for disposing the revisional application in terms of solenama by setting aside the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka allowing the case.

15. The aforesaid case was heard on 5-10-2005 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka and was pleased to allow the Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 on the basis of the solenama by setting aside the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 262 of 2005 by the Court of Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka.

16. Subsequently the plaintiff-petitioners transferred the suit land to one Mr Md Belayet Hossain by a registered sale deed being No. 4464 dated 30-10-2005 and handed over the possession of the suit land to him and in the said sale deed the defendant-opposite party No. 1 voluntarily put his signature as witness of the sale deed. Subsequently after disposing of Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 the defendant-opposite party No. 2 who was not an application of the above Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 before the trial Court and he having ceased to have any legal right in the suit land after dismissing of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002 on 18-1-2003 by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court on 9-11-2005 filed an application without any affidavit for setting aside the order dated 5-10-2005 behind the back of the plaintiff-petitioners and the learned District Judge committed error of law by re-opening the above civil revision and fixed the date on 15-11-2005 for hearing the application filed by the defendant-petitioner No. 2 subject to serving copy upon the plaintiff-petitioners.

17. Subsequently on 15-11-2005 the defendant-opposite party No. 1 filed an application behind the back of the plaintiff-petitioners before the District Judge for setting aside earlier order dated 5-10-2005 and to reject the solenama and the learned District Judge, Dhaka fixed the application for hearing on 21-11-2005. Subsequently after hearing the application on 22-11-2005 the learned District Judge recalled his earlier order dated 5-10-2005 and fixed on 30-11-2005 for hearing of Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 and on 30-11-2005 the learned District Judge, Dhaka dismissed the Civil Revision for default.

18. Thereafter on 19-3-2006 the plaintiff-petitioners and the defendant-opposite party No. 1 jointly filed an application for re-calling the order dated 22-11-2005 and 30-11-2005 for restoring the order dated 5-10-2005 and the learned District Judge, Dhaka allowed the application and restored the Civil Revision to its original file and number and fixed the date on 4-4-2006 for hearing of solenama. Thereafter the learned District Judge, Dhaka after hearing the Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 was pleased to reject the same without disposing the solenama filed by the parties by his judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 and thereby committed an error of law resulting an error in decision occasioning failure of justice. On receiving the judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 262 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 4 of 2000 filed by the plaintiff-petitioners on 9-5-2006 passed an order to issue writ for delivery of possession of the suit land in favour of the defendant-opposite party No. 1 and on the basis of the aforesaid order the defendant-opposite parties are trying to dispossess the vendee of the plaintiff-petitioners.

19. The plaintiff-petitioners took over the possession of the suit land under order of appropriate Court and possessing the same within the knowledge of defendant-opposite parties and others and an order was passed by the Appellate Division, Supreme Court on 20-6-2005 for staying operation of the judgment and order passed in Civil Revision No. 4754 of 2003 by the High Court Division for 6(six) months.

20. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka dismissing the revisional application and affirming the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka allowing the application of the defendant-opposite party No. 1 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 the plaintiff-petitioners preferred the instant revisional application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

21. The learned Counsel Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan with Mr Syed Mokkadas Ali, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners at the very outset of the hearing draws my attention to the order dated 23-3-2005 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 for revival of ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 and submits that in the context of the judgment passed by the highest judicial forum of Supreme Court, Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002 the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka is absolutely wrong and committed gross illegality by entertaining the application for revival of Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 since the matter has already been decided by the Appellate Division. Next he submits that thereafter the plaintiff preferred a revisional application before the learned District Judge, Dhaka being Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005. The learned District Judge, Dhaka after hearing the revision passed the order on 5-10-2005 stating that since both the parties jointly filed the solenama the revisional application was allowed and the order dated 23-3-2005 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 was set aside. Thereafter the defendant No. 2 Mizanur Rahman behind the back of the plaintiff filed an application on 9-11-2005 and prayed for stay operation of the order dated 5-10-2005, the learned District Judge, Dhaka fixed the date for hearing of the application on 15-11-2005. Thereafter on 10-11-2005 defendant No. 2-opposite party submitted another application stating, inter alia, that the copy of the application dated 9-11-2005 has been served upon the lawyer of the petitioner as such the date of hearing of the stay petition may kindly be heard expeditiously and the learned District Judge, Dhaka was pleased to hear the stay petition on the same day and allowed the petition stating that the order passed by him on 5-10-2005 has been stayed till 15-11-2005. Thereafter on 15-11-2005 opposite party No. 1 Abul Fayez Abdullah also appeared and submitted a petition for stay operation of the order dated 5-10-2005 and disposed of the matter after hearing both the parties. Hearing the opposite party Nos. 1-2 the learned District Judge, Dhaka fixed the date of hearing for stay petition and also to cancel the solenama fixed the date on 21-11-2005 and the order of stay extended up to that date. On 16-11-2005 opposite party No. 1 submitted another application for early hearing of the stay petition preferably on that date instead of 21-11-2005 because the copy of the petition has already been served upon the petitioner and the learned District Judge, Dhaka partly allowed the prayer and fixed the date for hearing of the stay petition on 17-11-2005. On 17-11-2005 opposite party Nos. 1-2 filed Hazira for hearing of the stay petition but the petitioner was not present in the Court. Since the learned Presiding Judge was on leave the hearing of the stay petition fixed on 22-11-2005. It appears from the order-sheet on 22-11-2005 opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 filed Hazira and the record was taken up for hearing and after hearing the stay petition the learned District Judge, Dhaka set aside the order dated 5-10-2005 passed by him earlier in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 and fixed the date for hearing of the revision on 30-11-2005. Thereafter on 30-11-2005 since the petitioner of the revision was not present and on the other hand, the opposite party Nos. 1-2 remains present in the Court by filing Hazira, the learned District Judge, Dhaka took up the matter for hearing and the revision was dismissed for default. Thereafter on 31-1-2006 the petitioner filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that the opposite party Nos. 1-2 behind the back of the petitioner by practicing fraud upon the Court and obtained an order on 22-11-2005 and 30-11-2005 canceling the earlier order dated 5-10-2005 and prayed for restoration of order dated 5-10-2005 and the date was fixed on 23-2-2006 for hearing of the application. Subsequently the opposite party No. 2 on 15-3-2006 filed a written objection against the application filed by the petitioner under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and prayed for time and the time was allowed and the date was fixed on 19-3-2006 for hearing of the petition. Thereafter on 19-3-2006 both the petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 1-3 jointly filed an application to the effect that the application filed by the petitioner dated on 31-1-2006 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to cancelled the order dated 22-11-2005 and 30-11-2005 for restoration of the order dated 5-10-2005 along with solenama be restored. The learned District Judge, Dhaka allowed the application under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and cancel the order dated 30-11-2005 and restored the Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 and fixed the date for hearing on 4-4-2006. Thereafter on 4-4-2006 opposite party No. 1 prayed for adjournment of the case and next date was fixed on 9-4-2006. Thereafter on 12-4-2006 the learned District Judge, Dhaka heard the Civil Revision No. 262 of 2004 and fixed the date on 16-4-2006 for order. On 16-4-2006 the learned District Judge, Dhaka dismissed the revision and affirmed the order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 and thereby set aside the ex parte judgment and decree dated 23-6-99 restoring the original suit to its original file and number. The learned Counsel Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan finally, submits that the learned District Judge, Dhaka acted illegally and committed error occasioning failure of justice because he cannot set aside his own order after signing the order finally he has become functus officio. The learned District Judge, Dhaka ought to have considered that in this checkered backdrop of the case, particularly where the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in their finding and decision in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002 in respect of the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 rejected the leave petition filed by the opposite parties. The learned District Judge, Dhaka ignoring the decision and finding of the Appellate Division and his own order passed on 5-10-20005 which was absolutely wrong and fallacious and liable to be interfered by this Court.

22. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Md Luthfe Alam, appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1, submits that the dispute between the parties was compromised out of the Court, as such, he will not contest the Rule and conceded to the argument advanced by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-petitioners, and he further submits that if the Rule is made absolute he has got no objection.

<u>23. On a meticulous examination of the Judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka and other connected papers and documents, particularly the judgments of the Appellate Division, it transpires that the impugned judgment dated 16-4-2006 passed by the learned District Judge is manifestly perverse. Because, the finding and decision of the Appellate Division is binding on all the courts below including the High Court Division under Article 111 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka is absolutely wrong, illegal and manifestly perverse which is liable to be set aside.</u>

<u>24. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case and the discussion made above I find substance in the submission of the learned Counsel Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan for the plaintiff-petitioners. Hence the judgment and order dated 16-4-2006 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, in Civil Revision No. 262 of 2005 dismissing the revisional application and affirming the judgment and order dated 23-3-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 by the learned Assistant Judge Nawabgonj, Dhaka, allowing the application of defendants Under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by setting aside judgment and ex parte decree dated 23-6-1999 and restoring the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 its original file and number is hereby set aside.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to the costs. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated. Lower court records be sent down at once.</u>

End.
