parties:
Abdul Matin ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Government of Peoples Republic of Bangladesh ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
In interest of justice it is felt to record a message that many litigants including the Government in order to steer clear of Order/ Judgment/Decree maintained by last ladder of hierarchy take recourse to ingenious methods in filing civil proceedings to rout order/ Judgment and decree of Courts including highest Court of the land. Seekers of Justice in whose favour Judicial verdict had been pronounced are to wait, wait and wait to be favoured ultimately with fruit of verdict and sometimes they become victims of justice in the hands of those litigants. The civil proceeding in hand is an apt paradigm how Judgment and Decree awarded in favour of defendant-petitioner of Civil Revision Case which had been maintained by Appellate Division rendering final touch has been ventured to be thwarted by opposite party who is no other than the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commissioner, Comilla.

2. Legal controversy attracting attention of this Revisional Court is a Judicial verdict recorded by learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 184 of 1985 overturning a Judicial decision rendered by learned Munsif now Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla in Title Suit No. 165 of 1985 accepting prayer made by petitioner who was first-defendant in the suit to reject the plaint under the provision engrafted in Order VII, rule 11 of The Code. Judgment of volte-face of learned Appellate Judge prompted defendant-petitioner to invoke this Court's Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged under section 115(1) of The Code on bestowing a Revision petition.

3. Portrayal of essential and requisite fact forming backdrop of Civil Revision case will be instructive in resolving war of words and those are succinctly put down hereunder:

a. Predecessor of defendant-petitioner Abdur Razzak as plaintiff laid a suit being Title Suit No. 136 of 1959 in the First Court of Munsif at Comilla seeking following reliefs:

i. Declaration of Rayati title on suit property described in second schedule to plaint and, also, for confirmation of possession therein.

ii. A decree of permanent injunction restraining first-defendant of the suit, Government of East Pakistan, represented by Collector, Tripura District from making any settlement elsewhere in respect of second schedule property.

b. Cadastral Survey Plot No. 596 covering an area of 4.04 acres corresponding to State Acquisition plot No. 1334, area being 3.967 (tank). 1328/1502, being area 10 acres and plot Nos. 1334/1507, being area .01 had been suit property.

c. Baluster of claim put forth by plaintiff was that he took settlement of suit tank plot No. 596 from Maharaja of Tripura by way of registered Patta deed dated 9-4-1951 and got possession thereof.

d. Suit was contested by First-Defendant-Government of East Pakistan.

e. Pleader Commissioner was appointed for holding Local Investigation in respect of suit property. Pleader Commissioner submitted a Report.

f. Suit was decreed in part on contest against defendant Government of East Pakistan. Plaintiff's title to portion of Suit property marked-"C" in Pleader Commissioner's Map had been declared and possession therein had been confirmed. First-defendant Government was restrained from making any settlement in respect of "C" marked portion of suit property to anybody else. Plaintiff's claim with respect to "A" and "B" marked portion of Suit property in Pleader Commissioner's Map stood dismissed.

g. Decree declaring right, title and interest in the Suit tank in Title Suit No. 136 of 1959 was confirmed in Title appeal.

h. Suit tank was acquired by Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) Comilla. Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla issued a Notice dated 1-10-1977 allegedly under sections 54(1) and 39(1) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Rules made thereunder stating that Government had acquired the suit tank under the provision of section 3 of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and directed Abdur Razzak, predecessor of defendant-petitioner, to submit returns for assessment of compensation for the suit tank. Abdur Razzak, predecessor of defendant-petitioner and one Abdul Matin instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 467 of 1977 in the Court of Munsif, Sadar, Comilla now Assistant Judge for a declaration that order of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) acquiring suit tank is illegal and void.

i. Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla and others as defendants put up contest against the suit on presentation of a written statement pressing into service contention that suit tank is a fishery and it was liable to be acquired by Government and Government legally acquired suit tank.

j. Learned Munsif dismissed suit adopting the view that suit tank was a fishery and it was liable to be acquired tinder section 3 of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and it had been legally acquired by Government.

k. Feeling aggrieved by aforesaid decision of learned Munsif an appeal, being Title Appeal No. 154 of 1980, before learned District Judge, Comilla had been carried. Learned Subordinate Judge heard the appeal, allowed it, reversed decision rendered by learned trial Judge and decreed suit rendering decision that suit tank was not liable to be acquired under Ordinance No. 12 of 1960 and it was a tank excavated by human hand and, also, that tank was not acquirable under section 3 of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

l. Against Judgment pronounced in Title Appeal, Government approached this Court in a Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code. Civil Revision Petition has been numbered as Civil Revision No. 1603 of 1981. Learned Single Judge heard Civil Revision Case and by Judgment dated May 31, 1984 discharged the Rule springing out of Civil Revision Petition. High Court Division in discharging the Rule came in full agreement with decisions recorded by learned Appellate Judge.

m. Termination of Civil Revision Case before High Court Division could not deter Government to make a halt. Government chose to carry controversy to Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 434 of 1984. Appellate Division by Judgment dated 14-2-1985 dismissed Leave Petition adopting the view that learned Judge of High Court Division committed no illegality in refusing to interfere with finding of fact arrived at by lower appellate Court which was passed on consideration of evidence. Legal controversy was ultimately laid at rest by highest court of the land i.e. Appellate Division of Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

n. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commissioner, Comilla once again mounted an endeavour to re-open controversy on institution of a suit being Title Suit No. 165 of 1985 in the Third Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Comilla seeking a declaration that alleged lease of suit land by Abdur Razzak from Maharaja of Tripura by an unilateral patta executed on 9-4-1951 and registered on 12-4-1951 is illegal, malafide, collusive, without jurisdiction, void and is of no legal effect and right, title and interest of plaintiff on suit land is not effected by it.

o. First defendant in suit, who is no other than son of Abdur Razzak, bestowed a petition under Order VII, rule 11 of The Code for rejection of plaint canvassing grounds that the war of words having been finally and conclusively determined by Court of First Instance which was maintained by highest court of the land i.e. Appellate Division, cannot be re-opened and reagitated in the suit and suit is barred by law i.e. by the Doctrine of res judicata.

p. Plaintiff-Government of Bangladesh contested petition laid under Order VII, rule 11 of The Code on laying a written objection.

q. Learned Munsif now Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla by order dated 15-8-1985 accepted petition of first-defendant and rejected plaint canvassing ground that the matter of which the present suit had been decided finally and materially by Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh cannot be raised. The other view which weighed with the learned Munsif in rejecting paint was that genuineness of settlement of defendant's predecessor in respect of suit land obtained from Maharaja of Tripura was finally decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh and finally decided point cannot be opened to avoid multiplicity of suits and cases.

r. Feeling aggrieved, plaintiff as appellant sought setting aside said adjudication rendered by learned Munsif now Assistant Judge through a medium of appeal being Title Appeal No. 184 of 1985 before learned District Judge, Comilla, Learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Comilla heard the appeal and by Judgment dated 22-7-2004 allowed it and knocked down Judgment recorded by learned Munsif.

s. First-defendant could not reconcile to verdict pronounced by learned Joint District Judge and ventilated his grievance in resorting to his Court's Civil Revisional Jurisdiction engrafted in section 115(1) of The Code on presentation of a Civil Revision Petition. First-defendant-petitioner shall be referred to hereinafter as defendant-petitioner.

4. Plaintiff-opposite party put up resistance to Civil Revision Petition on laying a Counter-Affidavit controverting statements made in Revision Petition. Basic contention tabled in Counter-Affidavit is that question of res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law and res judicata can be decided at the time of trial.

5. Contention pressed into service from side of defendant-petitioner is catalogued hereunder.

i. Title of first-defendant-petitioner had been declared and possession had been confirmed on suit tank in Title Suit No. 136 of 1951 as well as title Suit No. 467 of 1977 and decision rendered in both the suits in respect of acquisition of Title on the part of predecessor of first-defendant-petitioner on the strength of Patta deed from Maharaja of Tripura had been confirmed by High Court Division as well as Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and present suit is hit by the principle of res judicata and, also, of constructive res judicata and controversy, which was laid at rest finally by highest court of land i.e. Appellate Division, cannot be allowed to be re-opened by plaintiff-opposite party on laying a fraudulent, misconceived and fancy suit.

6. The kernel question that survives for determination in this Civil Revision Case is, whether the plaint presented by plaintiff-opposite party is liable to be rejected on the strength of provision envisaged in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

7. In approaching the question, law and principles of res judicata embodied in section 11 of The Code and/inherent power engrafted in section 151 of the Code may profitably be explored.

8. Doctrine of res judicata has received a  statutory sanction in The Code as a matter of prudence and to give due weightage to a  finding or decision so as to reach finality in the  matter of a dispute between the same parties  or litigating under the same parties. The Doctrine, thus, is to achieve finality of dispute between parties being a principle of prudence so as to give efficacy to a finding of Court rather than permit the parties go to trial more or less on the same issues over again. Judicial verdict has its special sanctity and cannot be subject matter of discussion at any future time involving identical or similar issues. Res judicata, thus, is a special form of estoppel.

9. Doctrine of res judicata or constructive res judicata predominantly is a principle of equity, good conscience and justice. In Carl-Zeiss Stiftung vs Rayner and Keeler Ltd and others = (1967) The Law Reports: Appeal Cases 853 = (1966) 2 All ER it has been aptly stated by Lord Upjohn: The broader principle of res judicata is founded on twin principles. So frequently expressed in Latin that there should be an end to litigation and justice demands that the same party shall not be harassed twice for the same cause.

10. Rule 11 of Order VII of the Code deals with power of Court to reject a plaint. Rule contemplates that still-born suit should be nipped in the bud at its inception so that no further time is consumed on a fruitless litigation. A suit which on the face of it is incompetent under law should not be allowed to further encumber legal proceedings. If the suit is barred by law it is the statutory duty of Court to reject plaint.

11. Section 151 of The Code does not formulate any new doctrine. It is only a Legislative recognition of well-known doctrine and principle that every Court has inherent power to act ex debito justitiae to do that real justice for administration of which alone it exists. Under section 151 of the Code Court acts ex debito justitiae according to equity, justice and good conscience and in consonance with fundamental principles of Judicial procedure. It has been ruled by Superior Courts of Sub-Continent that a plaint may be rejected under the provision of Order VII. rule 11 and if plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 same can be very well rejected in exercise of inherent power under section 151 of The Code.

12. Law on the subject has been spelt out, discussed and considered in good number of cases of our jurisdiction as well as foreign jurisdiction. Of those Burmah Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union and others, 18 DLR 709 may profitably be taken notice of High Court considered the rejection of plaint matter under the provision of Order VII, rule 11. It laid down the principle that a plaint can be thrown in liming if not under Order VII, Rule 11, then under Court's inherent power Murshed, CJ, speaking for the Court, observed at paragraph No. 10:

Order VII, rule 11 of The Code, as quoted above, enumerates certain categories under which the Court is called upon to reject a plaint, but, it is obvious that they are not exhaustive. It appears from the language of rule 11 of Order VII, that it requires that an incompetent suit should be laid at rest at the earliest moment so that no further time is wasted over what is bound to collapse as not being permitted by law.

It has been, also, laid down in paragraph No. 11:

A suit may be specifically barred by law and, in such an event, the matter would come under the express terms of clause (d) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code. But, even in a case where a suit is not permitted by necessary implication of law in the sense that a positive prohibition can be spelt out of legal provisions, the Court has an inherent jurisdiction to reject the plaint. This really amounts to saying that Order VII, rule 11, is not exhaustive. Hardly any authority is needed for such a proposition. I may, however, refer to some decisions on this point.

13. In suit in hand relief claimed by plaintiff-opposite party i.e. Government of Bangladesh, is that alleged lease of suit land by Abdur Razzak from Maharaja of Tripura by a unilateral patta executed on 9-4-1951 registered on 12-4-1951 is illegal, malafide, collusive, without jurisdiction, void and is of no legal effect and right, title and interest of the plaintiff is not affected by it. In Title Suit No. 136 of 1959 foundation of claim of Abdur Razzak, predecessor of defendant-petitioner was, patta deed dated 9-4-1951 from Maharaja of Tripura in respect of Suit Tank and title on suit tank had been declared by Court of First Instance. The said Judgment was, also, upheld in the Appeal carried by Government. Government remains fully satisfied with Judgment and decree and did not carry the issue neither before High Court Division nor before Appellate Division. In Title Suit No. 467 of 1977 the order passed by Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) acquiring the suit tank was struck down by the learned Appellate Judge in Title Appeal No. 154 of 1980 and the verdict pronounced in Title appeal was maintained by the High Court Division as well as by Appellate Division. The patta deed dated 9-4-1951 in favour of predecessor of defendant-petitioner by Maharaja of Tripura was accepted as valid patta deed by highest court of the land. Venture undertaken from the side of plaintiff-opposite party i.e. Government of Bangladesh, to reopen the issue which was finally and conclusively decided by judicial verdicts of last and highest Court of the country, cannot be allowed to be proceeded with and attempt by way of a presentation of a plaint is liable to be nipped in the bud at its inception so that no further time is consumed on a fruitless litigation.

14. In equity, good conscience and administration of justice as well as in interest of majesty of law and sanctity and finality of judicial verdicts of Superior Courts, provision engrafted in Order VII, rule 11 and section 151 of The Code is to be invoked and exercised to bury Title Suit No.165 of 1985 laid by plaintiff-opposite party at the threshold.

<u>15. Learned Munsif, Sadar Comilla as Court of First Instance approached controversy in right and proper direction and came to a correct decision in recording rejection of plaint. But the learned Joint District Judge as Appellate Judge totally misdirected his approach in resolving the war of words and committed a substantial error in overturning the decision rendered by learned Munsif and by the error a failure of justice has been occasioned.</u>

<u>16. Before parting, I am inclined to record an observation that no litigant including the Government got any right to lay fraudulent, shady, ill-motivated and untenable proceeding in a court of law when those cases are throttling the functioning of justice dispensation system which is itself groaning under unbearable arrears and backlogs and virtually gasping for breath.</u>

<u>17. Corollary thereof is that Rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code got merit. It succeeds. Rule is made absolute. Judgment and Decree dated 22-7-2004 passed by learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 184 of 1985 stands set aside/quashed and Judgment dated 15-8-1985 recorded by learned Munsif now Assistant Judge, Sadar, Comilla in Title Suit No. 165 of 1985 is restored.</u>

18. Stay granted by this Court stands vacated.

19. Regard being had to the fact and circumstances of the case, I direct the parties to bear their respective costs.

Lower Courts Records are sent down at once.

End.

lawyer:
Abdur Razzaque with Ehsan A Siddiq, Advocates-For the petitioner. 
Tufailur Rahman with Umme Salma, Advocates -For the Opposite Party No. 2
parties:
Smith Co-Generation (BD) Private Limited ------ Award-holder-Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh Power Development Board and Judgment another ------ debtor-Opposite party
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: This Rule calls in question an order No. 17 dated 27-8-2008 passed by the Court of District Judge, Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 4 of 2004 rejecting the application of the petitioner for vacating the Order No. 13 dated 27-9-2005 purportedly passed under Order XXI rule 29 of the Code Civil Procedure staying proceedings of the said Money Execution Case.

<u>2. Relevant facts, in short, are that the petitioner is a private limited company represented in Bangladesh through its constituted Attorney, Mr Md Habibur Rahman, Advocate, Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The petition participated in the tender for setting up a Barge Mounted Power Generation Plant in Bangladesh having the capacity of generating 500 MW of electricity and got the work by the opposite party No. 1, Bangladesh Power Development Board. Pursuant to the said tender, the petitioner entered into two sets of agreements with the Bangladesh Power Development Board, namely (i) a Power Purchase Agreement and (ii) a Land Lease Agreement and also submitted a Bank Guarantee to the opposite party No. 1 as security for carrying out the construction work. In terms of the said agreements the opposite party No. 2, the Government of Bangladesh was required to issue a number of permissions to the petition-company but the opposite party No. 2 having failed to issue the required permissions within the stipulated time as a result of which the commencement of the project was delayed. As such, the opposite party No. 1, Bangladesh Power Development Board declared that the petitioner had defaulted in carrying out of its obligations under the said Agreements and terminated the Power Purchase Agreement and Land Lease Agreement on 15-2-1999 and 17-2-1999 respectively. The opposite party No. 1 also encashed the Bank Guarantee submitted by the petitioner.</u>

<u>3. Being aggrieved thereby the petitioner initiated a arbitration proceedings against the opposite parties before the International Court of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC). The arbitration proceedings were commenced in accordance with the provisions of the said Agreements. The opposite party No. 1 participated in the arbitration proceedings by appointing its own arbitrator. The International Court of Arbitration after considering the claim of the respective parties passed Awards in favour of the petitioner on 11-9-2000, 8-3-2002, 2-9-2002 and 30-10-2003 respectively. Thereafter, the petitioner in order to enforce the Awards in Bangladesh on 10-8-2004 filed Money Execution case No. 4 of 2004 before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka for recovery of Taka 84,75,44,524.80 to together with interest in accordance with section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 2001.</u>

<u>4. The opposite party No. 1 entered appearance in the said Execution Case and on 28-11-2004 filed an application under Order XXI rule 29 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka for stay of the execution proceedings stating that the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff earlier instituted Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 before the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka challenging the legality of the Arbitral Awards passed by the International Court of Arbitration and, as such, it is required to stay all further proceeding of the Execution Case till disposal of the aforesaid two Title Suits.</u>

5. The Court of District Judge, Dhaka upon hearing the said application was pleased to stay all further proceedings of the said Execution Case pending disposal of Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 of 2004 by his order dated 27-9-20-05 stating as follows:

শোনা হল। দায়িক পক্ষ জারী মামলার কার্যক্রম স্থগিত রাখার জন্য প্রার্থনা করেছেন। ডিক্রিদার পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশুলী আপত্তি নেই উল্লেখ উক্ত দরখাস্তের মার্জিনে স্বাক্ষর করেছে। কাজেই দরখাস্তটি মঞ্জুর করা গেল। জারী মামলার কার্যক্রম বিজ্ঞ জেলা জজ ১ম আদালতে দেঃ মোঃ-৩৬৭/০০ ও দেঃ-৪০/০৪ মামলা নিস্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত স্থগিত করা গেল।

6. The petitioner-company after being unsuccessful in taking all possible efforts to get the aforesaid title suits heard, on 19-6-2008 filed an application for vacating the order of stay dated 27-9-2005 before the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka stating, inter-alia, that the learned District Judge, Dhaka had acted without jurisdiction in allowing the application for stay of the execution proceeding till disposal of Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 of 2004 pending before the leaned Joint District Judge, Dhaka. It has been also stated in the application that the consent of the lawyers cannot grant jurisdiction inasmuch as jurisdiction of a Court is created by statute, it can neither be conferred nor taken away by consent of the parties or their lawyers.

7. The opposite party No. 1 resisted the said application for vacating the order of stay by filing a written objection contending that the learned District Judge, Dhaka in the facts and circumstance of the case committed no illegality in allowing the application for stay all further proceedings of the Execution Case No. 4 of 2004 till disposal of Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 of 2004 by order dated 27-9-2005.

<u>8. The learned District Judge, Dhaka after hearing both the parties rejected the application of the petitioner for vacating the order of stay by the impugned order No. 17 dated 27-8-2008 mainly on, two grounds that the petitioner had not objected at the time of hearing the application for staying proceeding of the Execution Case No. 4 of 2004 pending disposal of Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 of 2004 and in the attending facts and circumstances of the case the complications may arise if the order of stay dated 27-9-2005 is vacated.</u>

<u>9. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid order dated 27-8-008 the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.</u>

10. Mr Abdur Razzaque, the learned Advocate appearing for the award-holder-petitioner submits that order XXI rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure clearly provides for staying the execution of a decree till the disposal of the pending suit is only attracted when the subsequent suit is pending before the same Court who passed the decree in the previous suit and it must be filed by the judgment debtor which is lacking in the present case but the Court of District Judge, Dhaka having failed to appreciate this simple legal aspect of the case and thereby seriously erred in law in passing the impugned order without properly applying his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and law bearing on the subject and the same has resulted in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Razzaque to fortify his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 4 BLC 615 and 53 DLR 610.

11. Mr Tufailur Rahman, the learned Advocate on the other hand appearing for the opposite party NO. 2 by filing counter affidavit support the impugned order which was, according to him just, correct and proper. He is the course of argument after placing the impugned order and other materials on record submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case the learned District Judge committed no illegality in allowing the application for staying all further proceedings of the execution case till disposal of the pending suits.

12. Now, let us examine first how far the learned District Judge, Dhaka was justified in allowing the application for staying all further proceedings of the execution case No. 4 of 2004 till disposal of the Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 of 2004 pending before the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka.

<u>13. It is found that the petitioner in order to enforce the Awards of the International Court of Arbitration in Bangladesh on 10-8-2004 filed Money Execution Case No. 4 of 2004 before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka for recovery of Taka 84,75,44,524.80 along with interest in accordance with section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and prior to the said Execution Case the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff had filed two separate suits being Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 of 2004 before the Joint District Judge, Dhaka Challenging the legality of the Arbitral Awards passed by the International Court of Arbitration. In this connection the relevant provisions of law are required to be referred to for having a better view of the dispute in question.</u>

14. Order XXI rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows:

"Where a suit is pending in any Court against the holder of a decree of such Court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the Court may, on such terms as to security or otherwise, as it things fit, stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided."

<u>15. From a reading of the above quoted provisions, it transpires that an application for staying the execution of a decree till disposal of the pending suit is only attracted when the subsequent suit is pending before the same Court who passed the decree in the previous suit and it must be filed by the judgment-debtor.</u>

16. In the case of Bangladesh Chemical. Industries Corporation vs Eastern Bank Ltd reported in 4 BLC 615, it has been held that:

"It is thus manifestly clear that the two Courts are not the same Courts by are different Courts with defined jurisdiction. So, it is evident that Order XXI rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case."

17. In the case of Golam Rabbani Khandaker vs Hamida Bewa Shamsul Sheikh reported in 53 DLR 610, it has been held as follows:

"I read again the provision of rule 29 of Order XXI of the Code. It says "where a suit is pending in any Court against the holder of a decree of such Court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the Court may, on such terms as to security or otherwise as it thinks it, stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided. "This power has been clearly given to an Executing Court as well as to the Court in which suit impeaching the decree is pending if the decree is a decree of this Court."

<u>18. In this case we have already noticed that the Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and title Suit No. 40 of 2004 are pending before the joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka and the Arbitral Awards sought to be enforced by the District Judge has been passed by the International Court of Arbitration which is different from the Court before whom the aforesaid suits are pending Moreover, in order to invoke Order XXI rule 29 Of the Code of Civil Procedure, the existence of a decree is required and admittedly, the Arbitral Award sought to be enforced is neither a decree nor the same has been deemed to be a decree by any law. Therefore, in the facts of the case and the principles enunciated in the cited decisions vis-à-vis the provision of Order XXI rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure we have no hesitation to hold that the learned District Judge, Dhaka committed serious error of law in passing, the impugned order without property applying his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and law bearing on the Subject and the same has resulted in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.</u>

19. Now, it remains for us to consider the last submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2.

20. Mr Tufailur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2, Upon referring to the order sheets of the learned District Judge, Dhaka submits that the learned District Judge was pleased to allow the application for staying all further proceedings of the Money Execution Case No. 4 of 2004 till disposal of the Title Suit No. 367 of 2002 and Title Suit No. 40 of 2004 by his order dated 27-9-2005 mainly on the basis of the consent of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and thereafter, keeping silent over a period of two years and nine months it does not lie in the mouth of the petitioner that the Court of learned District Judge having failed to consider whether it has jurisdiction to pass the Order of Stay under Order XXI rule 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

21. In reply, Mr Razzaque relying on the decisions reported in 36 DLR (AD) 1 and 36 DLR (AD) 179 submits that when the law was conferred jurisdiction expressly, no amount of consent by the parties can invest a Court with jurisdiction which is not given by law.

22. To resolve this dispute we have studied the cited decision to the best of our ability and find in those decision our Appellate Division consistently held that the jurisdiction of Courts is created by statutes and that it can neither be conferred nor taken away by agreement or concession of parties to the litigation or of their lawyers. So, we are unable to see eye to eye to such submission made by Mr Tufailur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2.

23. Mr Abdur Razzaque, the learned Advocate at the fag end of the hearing upon referring to the provision of section 45 and 46 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 submits that learned District Judge also having failed to consider that the application for stay dated 27-9-2005 was not maintainable inasmuch as the execution case was filed in accordance with section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 which is a special Act and in that view of the matter the enforcement and execution of an Arbitral Award was required to be challenged in accordance with the provisions of the section 46 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. He adds that since there being remedy available under the special law, the remedy under general law is not entertainable.

<u>24. On a careful examination of section 45 and 46 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 it appears that there is a forum for seeking remedy against the execution of an Arbitration Award but the opposite party No. 1 without making an application under section 46 of the Arbitration Act made an application under Order XXI, rule 29 of the Code. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case vis-à-vis the provision of section 46 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 the grievance of the learned Advocate for the petitioner does not appear to be without substance.</u>

<u>25. For the reasons stated above, we are inclined to hold that the learned District Judge seriously erred in law in passing the impugned order without properly applying his judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and law bearing on the subject and the same has resulted in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.</u>

26. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned order dated 27-8-2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 4 of 2004 rejecting the application of the petitioner for vacating the order of stay is set-aside and accordingly, the order of stay dated 27-9-2005 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka is vacated.

Communicate this judgment at once.

End.

lawyer:
Moudud Ahmed with Raji Uddin Ahmed and Tas Miah Prodhan, Advocates—For the Petitioner.

Md Abul Kalam Patwary, Advocate—For the Opposite Party Nos. 2-4.
parties:
Babul Chandra Sheel ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Rupali Bank Ltd & others ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 17-5-2012 passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 28 of 2012 affirming the order No. 58 dated 28-4-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2006 arising out of Artha Rin Jari Case No. 183 of 2003 should not be set-aside.

2. The facts leading to the filing of this Revision, in brief, as follows:

The opposite party No. 1, Rupali Bank Limited as plaintiff instituted a mortgage suit being Mortgage Suit No. 67 of 1999 before the Artha Rin Adalat -1, Chittagong for realization of its loan of Taka 82,33,209-90 along with interest. The suit was ultimately decreed in favour of the bank. The judgment debtors having failed to pay the decreetal amount whereupon, the Bank filed Artha Rin jari Case No. 183 of 2003 for execution of the said decree. Thereafter, the decree holder bank in court process floated Tender on 18-10-2003 published in two daily news papers namely, Daily Khabar and Daily Azadi for auction sale of the immovable mortgaged property mentioned in the schedule and the petitioner and two others participated in the auction sale of the said mortgaged property. Among the other participants one of them offered Taka 80,000 and other Taka 1,20,000 in which the petitioner was selected as the highest bidder in the competitive auction sale on his offer Taka 4,00,000 (4 Lac) and, the Artha Rin Adalat on 18-10-2003 accepted the offer of the petitioner being the highest offer and directed the petitioner to deposit the entire bid amount and sale fees. The petitioner then deposited the rest of the bid amount and sale fee Taka 4,010. In this backdrop on 28-10-2003 the decree holder Bank filed an application under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Civil Procedure Code for setting-aside the auction sale. The Artha Rin Adalat upon hearing the parties rejected the application on 28-10-2003 and fixed the next date on 19-11-2003 for confirmation of the auction sale and the Executing Court after considering all the circumstances and evidence on record passed an order on 19-11-2003 confirming the auction sale.

3. In this background opposite party No. 1, Rupali Bank preferred an appeal before this Court being First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 151 of 2004 against the order dated 19-11-2003 and ultimately, a Division Bench of this Court disposed of the said appeal with the direction to the Artha Rin Adalat to register the petition filed by the plaintiff bank under order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure as Miscellaneous Judicial Case and to dispose of the same after hearing both the sides within 60 days from the date of receipt of the order. The learned Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong then in compliance of the order of this Court registered the case as Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2006, who after hearing both the parties by order dated 28-4-2010 allowed the Misc. Case and thereby set-aside the auction sale of the mortgaged property.

4. The unsuccessful petitioner, thereupon, preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 28 of 2012 before the learned District Judge, Chittagong who by his judgment and order dated 17-5-2012 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the order No. 58 dated 28-4-2010 passed by the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong in Misc. Case No. 4 of 2006 and the instant Revision application is directed against that judgment.

5. Mr Moudud Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in the course of his argument upon placing the relevant materials on record including the order dated 19-11-2003 passed by Artha Rin Adalat confirming the auction sale submits that both the Courts below erred in law in cancelling the auction sale dated 19-11-2003 without properly considering the facts of the case and the case made out by the petitioner and the same has occasioned failure of justice. He next submits that the impugned judgments of both the Courts below are perverse being contrary to law, evidence and materials on record in as-much as Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure enables the Court to interfere if fraud or any irregularity found in auction process but in this case there is nothing on record to suggest that any fraud or irregularity took place in auction process and it is apparent from the record that the Artha Rin Adalat after exhausting all the legal formalities confirmed the auction sale by its order dated 19-11-2003 and, as such, the judgments of both the Courts below are liable to be set-aside. Mr Moudud Ahmed further submits that both the courts below having failed to take into consideration that a great fraud has been committed by the judgment Debtor-Opposite party Nos. 3-6 in collaboration with the bank in obtaining a loan amounting to Taka 82,33,209.90 by providing the only security of the schedule property for the aforesaid loan, the petitioner as a bonafide auction purchaser has purchased the schedule property in the auction sale by offering the highest rate which is 7 (seven) times more than the mouza rate and thereby fell into an error of law resulting in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice.

6. Drawing my attention to the list of Mouza rate under Hathazari Sub-registry office as evidenced by "Annexure-D" to the revisional application Mr Moudud Ahmed argues that at the time of the auction sale the Government market value of the lower land (Nal Jomi) at Mouza Mithachora under Hathazari upazila, District Chittagong was Taka 3,499 per decimal and the petitioner has paid Taka 25,000 per decimal in total Taka 4,00,000 for the mortgaged land, that is, seven times more than the Mouza rate so, the plea as canvassed by the opposite party No. 1, Rupali Bank Limited in collusion with the judgment-debtors that the auction price of the mortgaged property was shockingly low is untrue and without any legal basis.

7. Mr Moudud Ahmed while elaborating his submission referred to the decision reported in 15 MLR (AD) 21 = 62 DLR (AD) 231 and submits that the proposition of law is by now well settled that execution proceedings ends with the completion of auction process in respect of the mortgaged property and once an auction sale is complete no relief is available against such auction sale but the mortgagee may proceed against the mortgagor bank for any compensation if it is proved that there was illegality in the auction sale and in this case it is apparent from the record that the Artha Executing Court confirmed the auction sale by its order dated 19-11-2003 in accordance with law as there was no allegation of fraud or irregularities in the auction sale process but both the Courts below misconceived the facts of the case and the law bearing on the subject and thereby wrongly set-aside the auction sale confirmation order dated 19-11-2003.

8. Mr SM Harmuz Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, by filing counter affidavit contested the Rule. He submits that both the Courts below were perfectly justified in setting-aside auction sale inasmuch as actual price of the mortgaged property is far from Taka 4,00,000 and thereupon, the loan defaulter, the proprietor of M/S NG Corporation, Gobinda Chandra Sarker has signed and submitted an undertaking on non-judicial stamp of Taka 150 that if the loan is exempted, he is ready to pay a sum of Taka 40,00,000 for the schedule property. Finally, Mr Harmuz Ahmed submits that the opposite party No. 1, Rupali Bank Ltd, Andarkella Branch, Chittagong shall sustain irreparable loss and injury if the petitioner is allowed to purchase the mortgaged property only at Taka 4,00,00 in the name of the highest bidding as the same is repugnant to the provision of Section 33(2) Ga of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. The judgment of both the Courts below are well founded in law and facts and the same should not be disturbed.

9. Mr Md Abul Kalam Patwary, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 2-5 (judgment debtors) at the very outset adopting the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1, Rupali Bank Ltd. submits that the highest bid money amounting to Taka 4,00,000 is shockingly low from the actual price of the mortgaged property and opposite party Nos. 2-5 are ready to pay a sum of Taka 4,00,000 for getting back their mortgaged property.

10. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the revisional application, judgments of two Courts below, counter affidavit dated 8-12-2012 filed by the opposite party No. 1 and counter affidavit dated 10-1-2013 filed by the opposite party Nos. 2-5 and other materials on record. Now, to appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties from a correct angle let me first look whether Artha Rin Adalat committed any illegality in confirming auction sale by its order dated 19-11-2003.

11. I have carefully examined the materials on record, it appears that the decree holder bank in Court process floated Tender on 18-10-2003 published in two Bengali news papers namely, Daily Khabar and Daily Azadi for auction sale of the immovable mortgaged property as described in the schedule under the provision of section 33(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 in which the petitioner and two others participated in depositing 25% of the bidding money with the quotation in favour of the Court and among the other participants one of them offered Taka 80,000 and other Taka 1,20,000 and the petitioner was selected as the highest bidder in the competitive auction sale on his offer Tk 4,00,000 (4 Lac) . The Artha Rin Adalat on 18-10-2003 accepted the offer of the petitioner being the highest offer and directed the petitioner to deposit the rest of the bid money and sale fees. The petitioner then deposited the rest of the amount of Taka 3,00,000 and sale fee Tk. 4010 and then on 28-10-2003 the decree holder Bank filed an application under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Civil Procedure Code for setting-aside the sale on the ground that the bidding amount is shockingly low which can not be considered at all a fair price in view of the existing market price of the mortgaged property.

12. The Artha Rin Adalat after hearing the parties by its order dated 28-10-2003 rejected the application and fixed the next date on 19-11-2003 for confirmation of the auction sale. The Artha Rin Adalat after hearing the parties and on considering the materials on record and mouza rate under Hathazari Sub-registry office rejected the application by its order no. 18 dated 28-10-2003 on the finding that there was no illegality or irregularity in auction sale proceedings. It further appears from the Mouza rate of Mouza-Mithachhra under the Hathazari Sub-registry office, Chittagong ( Annexure-D-1) that the value of low land was Taka 34,900 per decimal and the petitioner offered Taka 25,000 per decimal in total 4,00,000 for the said land which is 7 (seven) times more than the Mouza rate.

13. On a query by me the learned Advocate for the opposite party-bank has found himself unable to refute the contention raised by Mr Moudud Ahmed that the petitioner offered Taka 25,000 per decimal in total 4,00,000 for the suit land which is 7 (seven) times more than the Mouza rate under Hathazari Sub-registry office and no illegality or irregularity took place in the auction sale proceedings. He, however, sought to argue that the courts below were perfectly justified in allowing the Misc. case and setting-aside the auction sale. Therefore, I am constrained to hold that the learned judge of the Artha Executing Court on the facts of the case and on consideration of the legal position rightly confirmed the auction sale after rejecting the application under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Civil Procedure Code for setting aside the auction sale filed by the decree holder bank.

14. Now, let me look at the more important question whether the Courts below were justified in setting-aside the auction sale of the mortgaged property on the finding that the highest bidder offered only an amount of Taka 4,00,000 which is very low than the existing market price of the valuable mortgaged property.

15. To resolve this dispute, provisions of Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure are required to be referred to for having a better view of the dispute in question. Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows:

"90—(1) Where any immoveable property has been sold in execution of a decree, the decree-holder, or any person entitled to share in a rateable distribution of assets, or whose interests are affected by the sale, may apply to the Court to set-aside the sale on the ground of a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting it:

Provided that no sale shall be set-aside on the ground of irregularity or fraud unless upon the facts proved the Court is satisfied that the applicant has sustained substantial injury by reason of such irregularity or fraud."

16. From the above, it is clear that no sale shall be set-aside on the ground of irregularity or fraud unless upon the facts proved the Court is satisfied that the applicant has sustained substantial injury by reason of such irregularity or fraud.

17. As I have already noticed that the decree holder bank filed an application under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Civil Procedure Code for setting-aside the auction sale and the learned Artha Rin Adalat-1, Chittagong rejected the application on the ground that the auction purchaser is the highest bidder and he deposited the entire bidding money and sale fees in time and the auction process has been conducted in presence of the decree holder bank and there was no allegation of fraud or irregularities in the auction sale process. Subsequently, the self same ground has been urged before the Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong by the decree holder bank as was done before the Artha Executing Court though the learned judge of the Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong allowed the application of the decree holder Bank filed under Order XXI, Rule 90 in Misc. Case No. 4 of 2006 and set-aside the auction sale of the mortgage property on the findings that the highest bidder offered only an amount of TK. 4,00,000 which is very low than the existing market price of the valuable mortgaged property and the decree holder Rupali Bank raised objection against accepting such offer due to very low offer.

18. In appeal, the Court of appeal below by the impugned judgment and order dated 17-5-2012 affirmed the said order of the Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong on the finding that there is sufficient materials on record to come to the decision which has been arrived at by the Court below.

19. On a careful perusal of the entire order sheets of the Artha Executing Court, I find no allegation of fraud or irregularities in the auction sale process of the mortgage property. The Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong on the facts of the case and on consideration of the legal position by its order dated 28-10-2003 rejected the application under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Civil Procedure Code for setting-aside the auction sale filed by the decree holder bank. A few lines of the said order reads as follows :

“শুনিলাম নথিসহ ডিক্রীদার পক্ষের দাখিলী দরখাস্ত দেখিলাম । দেখা যাইত্তেছে যে, বিগত ১৮-১০-০৩ ইং তারিখ অত্র জারী মামলার তপশীলের সম্পত্তি নিলাম ৰিক্রয়ের দিন ধার্য ছিল । উক্ত তারিখ ৩(তিন) জন দরদাতা দরপত্র দাখিল করিয়া নিলাম বিক্রয় অংশ গ্রহন করে । তৎমধ্যে বাবুল চন্দ্র শীল কর্তৃক দাখিলী ৪,০০,০০০ টাকার দরপত্র খানি সর্বোচ্চ হওয়ায় ইহা গৃহীত হয় ৷ বিধিমত সর্বোচ্চ দরদাতা নির্ধারিত সময়ের মধ্যে sale fee ও নিলামের সমৃদয় মূল্য পরিশোধ করিয়াছেন । ধার্য্য তারিখে নিলাম বিক্রয় কার্যক্রম ডিক্রীদারের উপস্থিতিতে সম্পন্ন হইয়াছে । নিলাম বিক্রয় কার্যক্রম আইন মোতাবেক পরিচালিত হওয়ায় উহাতে কোন অনিয়ম অথবা প্রতারণার উত্তর হইয়াছে মর্মে প্রতীয়মান হয় না বিধায় ডিক্রীদারের অত্রদরখাস্ত বিবেচনায় যোগ্য নহে । কাজেই ডিক্রীদারের অত্র দরখাস্ত না মঞ্জুর করা হইল ৷ আগামী ২১-১ ১-০৩ ইং তারিখ নিলাম স্থায়ীকৱণ (confirm) আদেশ প্রচারের জন্য দিন ধার্য্য করা হইল।

This finding is one of fact based on correct evaluation of the facts and materials on record.

20. It is clear from the above quoted finding of the Artha Executing Court that there was no fraud or irregularities in the auction sale process and the auction sale of the mortgaged property was held in accordance with law. The Artha Executing Court after having exhausted all procedure under the Am confirmed the auction sale by its order dated 19-11-2003. I do not think therefore that both the courts below made a correct approach to the simple problem. Besides, on top of that admittedly the petitioner offered Taka 25,000 per decimal in total Taka 4,00,000 for the suit land which is 7 (seven) times more than the Mouza rate under Hathazari sub-registry office, District Chittagong. Both the Courts below without comparing the bidding price with the Mouza rate of the local sub-registry office came to an erroneous finding that the highest bidder offered only an amount of Taka 4,00,000 which is very low than the existing market price of the valuable mortgaged property which resulted in the failure of justice.

<u>21. Thus evidently auction sale having taken place and sale having been confirmed by the Artha Rin Adalat after rejecting an application under Order XXI, rule 90 Code of civil Procedure filed by the decree holder bank as there was no allegation of fraud or irregularities in the auction sale process. Under such circumstances both the Courts below without existence of the legal requirements as laid down in Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code acted illegally in allowing the Misc. Case under the said rule for setting-aside the auction sale and the same has occasioned failure of justice.</u>

22. In the case of Sonali Bank vs Artha Rin Adalat and others reported in 15 MLR (AD) 21 = 62 DLR (AD) 231, it has been held as follows:—

"We have perused the writ petition as well as the order dated 2-1-2005 and 9-1-2005 passed in Mortgaged Execution Case No. 8 of 1995 and the judgment and order passed in the writ petition and considered the submission made by the learned Advocate appearing for the leave petitioner. It appears that the leave petitioner bank is negligent in not informing the executing Court about the fact of restoration of the rule and stay dated 15-6-2006 and that the leave petitioner bank by filing an application on 25-6-2006 prayed for receiving the pay order submitted by the auction purchaser in Court and it appears from the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division that the leave petitioner bank has already encashed the pay order and thereby accepted the auction sale. In view of the provision of law to the effect that once an auction is complete no relief is available against such auction sale but the mortgagee may proceed against the mortgagor bank for any compensation, if it is proved that there was illegality in the auction sale. In the instant case, it is not such case rather it appears that at the instant of the decree holder bank auction was held and ultimately the decree holder bank has withdrawn the money deposited by the auction purchaser. After the auction process is completed, proceeding with the execution case is redundant."

<u>23. From the above, I find a clear view of the law as it stands today that once an auction sale is complete no relief is available against such auction sale but the mortgagee may proceed against the mortgagor bank for any compensation, if it is proved that there was illegality in the auction sale.</u>

24. In this case I have already indicated that the auction purchaser was the highest bidder, who deposited the entire bidding money and sale fees in time as per order of the executing Court and the auction process has been conducted in presence of the decree holder bank and there was no allegation of fraud or irregularity or illegality in the auction sale process. Therefore, I am inclined to hold that both the courts below committed wrong in holding that the highest bidder appellant offered only an amount of Taka 4,00,000 which was very low than the existing market price of the valuable mortgaged property without comparing the bidding price with the Mouza rate of the local sub-registry office and without applying its judicial mind into the facts and circumstances of the case and law bearing on the subject and the same has resulted in an error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The contentions raised by the learned Advocates on behalf of the opposite parties for the aforesaid reasons are of no substance.

25. Incidentally, it may be mentioned that the grievance of Mr Moudud Ahmed to the effect that both the Courts below having failed to take into consideration that a great fraud has been committed by the judgment Debtor-Opposite Parties Nos. 3-6 in collaboration with the Bank in obtaining a loan amount of Taka 82,33,209.90 by providing the only security of the schedule property for the aforesaid loan in the facts and circumstance of the case does not appear to be without any substance.

26. In view of my discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs it is by now clear that the instant Rule must succeed.

27. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 17-5-2012 passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong in Misc. Appeal No. 28 of 2012 and the order No. 58 dated 28-4-2010 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong in Misc. Case No. 4 of 2006 are set-aside and the order dated 19-11-2003 passed by the Artha Execution Court in Artha Rin jari Case No. 183 of 2003 is restored.

Let a copy of this judgment be communicated to the Courts concerned at once.

End.

Syed Mokaddas Ali with Biswajit Chakraborty, Advocates--For the Petitioners. 
Zulfiqur Ahmed, Advocate--For Opposite Party Nos. 2.
parties:
Abdul Jabbar Bhuiyan and others ------ Petitioners
Vs
Kulsum Banu Bibi and others ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-2 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2006 and 7-2-2006 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria, in Title Appeal No. 7 of 2005 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 16-10-2004 and 21-10-2004 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria, in Title Suit No. 28 of 2004 dismissing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The opposite party Nos.1, Kulsum Banu Bibi, 2. Tara Banu Bibi and 3. Md Abdur Rahim as plaintiffs instituted the Title Suit No. 52 of 1991 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria impleading the above petitioner and others as defendants praying for a declaration that the compromise decree dated 8-11-90 passed in Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 is not binding upon them and the suit was subsequently transfer-red and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 53 of 1998 and lastly it was transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 28 of 2004 for trial.

3. That the case of the plaintiffs-opposite parties in brief are that Pandit Chandra Rudra Paul and Swarup Chandra Paul were original owners of the suit land of schedule No. 1 and while they were possessing and enjoying the property Kushai Chandra Das and Aswini Kumar Das purchased the same from them and became the owner and possessor of the land. Aswini Kumar Das died leaving behind 4 sons Ambika Charan Das, Paresh Das, Animesh Das and Amalesh Das and Kushai Chandra Das died leaving behind 2 sons Anil Chandra Das and Monindra Chandra Das and accordingly, RS Khatian No. 43 was prepared in their name. Ambika Charan Das and others while they were possessing and enjoying the property in the year 1963 they exchanged the said land with the land of one Moulavi Abdul Matin of Kasharmara Mouza of Police Station Radhakishorepur of Tripura, India and in this way Abdul Ma tin became owner and possessor of the schedule land. Moulvi Abdul Ma tin while owning and possessing the land on 28-12-64 exchanged .39 acres of land with plaintiff No. 1 and her husband Badsha Mia became owner and possessor of the same. In this way the plaintiff became owner of 0.39½ acres i.e. 0.39½ acres by exchange and 0.15 acres by purchase and thereafter sold 0.20 acres to plaintiff No. 2 who remained owner and possessor of rest 0.14½ acres of land.

4. Badsha Mia while owning and possessing 0.19½ acres of land along with others permitted defendant No. 2 to reside there temporarily as he became 'Peer' of Badsha and Badsha was his Murid as religious guide. Tara Banu opposite party No. 2 got her 0.04 acres of land as heirs. Subsequently Chan Mia and Jarina Begum and other heirs of Badsha Mia sold 0.12 acres of land to Tara Banu and in her way Tara Banu became the owner and possessor of 0.16 acres of land and when Nawab Mia husband of Tara Banu went to the Tahshil office for separation of Jama after paying rent on 10-1-91 then came to know that the defendant No. 2 vide Mutations Case No. 354/85-86 mutated his name in respect of 0.54 acres of land in Plot Nos. 166, 167 and 168. Thereafter the plaintiff on 21-1-1991 went to the office of Assistant Commissioner, Akhaura and came to know that a review case was pending against the said mutation case, then the plaintiff filed an application thereon for addition of party and Assistant Commissioner directed the parties to appear before him with necessary papers but the defendant No. 2 failed to show any papers in support of their title, that on 13-2-1991 the defendant No. 2 expressed that his brother-in-law, the defendant No. 1, was the owner of the land on the basis of the title suit and prayed for affirming the order of mutation, on 16-2-1991. The husband of plaintiff No. 1 searched for the suit and on 12-3-1991 after getting certified copy of the same came to know about the collusive compromise judgment and decree of the Title Suit No. 78 of 1988. The plaintiffs of the suit are the owners and possessors of the suit land knowing fully well that the plaintiffs of the instant suit land filed the Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 without making the plaintiffs as parties of the said suit and, as such, prayed for a decree that the compromise decree dated 8-11-1990 passed in Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 was collusive and not binding upon him.

5. The defendant Nos. 1-2(Ka)-2(Ja) contested the said suit by filing two separate sets of written statement denying all the material allegation of the plaint. The case of the defendant No. 1, in short, is that the original owner of the land was Ambika Charan Das and others and they sold the property to defendant No. 1 as at that time there was some restrictions in registration of minority properties, as such, a bainapatra was executed and the defendant No. 1 paid the rent to the Government and the brother-in-law (sister's husband) of defendant No. 1 used to possess and enjoy the suit land by erecting houses and establishing a Madrasha therein. That Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 was decreed on compromise with defendant No. 2 was rightly and properly passed and, as such, the instant suit should be dismissed.

6. The defendant Nos. 2(Ka)-2(Ja) also contested the suit by filing separate written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint stating, inter alia, that the defendant No. 2 Moulvi Deen Mohammad was a great Alem, he was the Khalifa of Sonakanda Darbar who had many disciples, the plaintiffs' predecessor Badsha Mia was also a Murid of defendant No. 2 and sold the land to defendant No. 2 by a registered deed No. 6699 dated 25-11-68 and on the same date executed a registered compensation deed No. 6700. Consequently, the defendant No. 2 during his lifetime had been living in the suit land by erecting houses and lived therein with his family and also established a Madrasha set up tube-well, latrine, etc. When the defendant No. 1 claimed the suit land and filed the Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 against the original owners, the defendant No. 2 filed a solehnama to get a compromise decree then the aforesaid compromise decree was passed. The plaintiff's predecessors Badsha Mia had no right title and possession in the suit land and in the recent survey operation when surveyor found defendant No. 2 in the suit land he prepared RS Khatian in his name correctly and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.

7. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria during the course of trial framed 5 issues.

1. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form?

2. Whether the suit is barred by limitation?

3. Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties?

4. Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get a decree as prayed for and

5. Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get any other relief.

8. The plaintiff examined as many as 6 witnesses and defendant examined as many as 4 witnesses to prove their respective cases.

9. During the pendency of the trial the plaintiff No. 3 Md Abdur Rahim submitted a compromise application stating, inter alia, that he will not contest the suit and he relinquished his claim over 20 decimals of the suit land bearing Plot Nos. 166 and 167.

10. The learned trial Court after concluding the trial examined the evidence on record and after perusing the exhibits, papers and documents dismissed the suit.

11. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the plaintiff No. 1. Kulsum Banu, the wife of Badsha Mia and plaintiff No. 2 Tara Banu, the daughter of Badsha Mia filed an appeal before the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria being Title Appeal No. 7 of 2005, the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria himself heard the title appeal and allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 31-1-2006 and 3-2-2006 respectively.

12. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria the defendant-respondent-petitioner preferred the instant revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court Division and obtained the present Rule.

13. The learned Counsel Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali with Mr Biswajit Chakraborty, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-petitioner, submits that the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria was absolutely wrong and erroneous in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned trial Court, after examining the evidence on record and discussing all the issues framed by him whether the suit is maintainable in its present form or not and other issues, passed the judgment and decree dismissing the suit of the plaintiff which was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Next he submits that the learned trial Court committed no error in. deciding the issues and rightly held that the plaintiff miserably failed to prove the case, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court was absolutely right and justified which should not be assailed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali next submits that the lower appellate Court while reversing the finding of the trial Court he should assign a cogent and reasonable ground and the finding of the trial Court should be reversed with reference to the evidence on record, but the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria committed a gross illegality in not referring the finding of the trial Court, particularly with regard to the law point which is liable to be set aside and interfered by this Court. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali further submits that the finding of the trial Court, particularly on 2 points, that the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the plaintiff No. 2 during the pendency of the trial of the suit by submitting a compromise petition and relinquished his claim over 20 decimals of the suit land in Plot Nos. 166-167 and accordingly, the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 ought to have corrected the schedule of the suit land. But the lower appellate Court did not mention a single word in his judgment on these two points i.e. with regard to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the compromise petition filed by the plaintiff No. 2 who has relinquished his claim and also did not file any appeal. This sort of non-consideration in finding of the lower appellate Court in reversing the judgment of the trial Court appears to be manifestly perverse which is liable to be interfered by this Court. The learned Counsel finally submits that admittedly the defendants had been in possession of the suit land since long so in a suit for declaration without seeking a consequential relief for recovery of khas possession is not at all maintainable. The PWs 2 and 3 in cross-examination categorically stated in their evidence that Deen Mohammed, the defendant No. 2, had been living in the suit land with his family members by erecting houses. PW 3 further stated in his evidence that defendant No. 2 Deen Mohammad was a good man and he was in possession of the suit land. He also submits that the lower appellate Court did not at all discuss the evidence of PWs and DWs. Md Ruhul Amin, son of Deen Mohammad was examined as DW 1 and after the death of Deen Mohammad during the pendency of the suit who was living in the suit land categorically stated in his evidence about the title and possession of the suit land and exhibited the registered title deed in original dated 25-11-68 which was exhibited as Exhibit-Ka. The registered deed Exhibit-Ka, the original purchase deed of the defendant obviously shows that the vendor of that deed Kulsum and Tara Banu along with others were the vendor who are now plaintiff Nos. 1-3 respectively and in that deed the vendee was Deen Mohammad the defendant No. 2 and since the purchase of the suit land in the year 1968 after the death of Badsha Mia the defendant has been living in the suit land with his other family members.

The learned lower appellate Court did not at all consider the evidence of DW with regard to the title deed and also the proof of possession of the defendant which was admitted by PWs 2 and 3, as such, the defendant successfully proved the title and possession in the suit land. Therefore, the learned trial Court properly dismissed the suit which was absolutely correct and justified. The finding of the appellate Court in reversing the finding of the trial Court transpires to be manifestly perverse which is liable to be interfered by this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and hence the Rule should be made absolute. The learned Counsel, before conclusion of his argument in support of his contention made above, referred the case of Nurul Islam (Babul) vs Shanti Rani Dhupi and others reported in 12 MLR (AD) 105 wherein it has been stated:

"Specific Relief Act (I of 1877)

Section 42. When the plaintiff is not in possession of suit land no decree for declaration of title can be granted without seeking for recovery of possession".

14. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Zulfiqur Ahmed, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party, submits that the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria was absolutely right and justified in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court which is not liable to be disturbed in revision by the High Court Division. Next he submits that the appellate Court, after discus-sing the evidence on record and perusing the exhibits, papers and documents produced by both the parties and after proper assessment of the evidence on record, came to his finding that the plaintiff could be able to prove the case successfully, as such, the suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiff. He further submits that the finding of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is final which is not liable to be disturbed by this Court. He also submits that the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria elaborately discussed the evidence on record and also found that the defendant on the basis of a forged solehnama decree tried to establish his claim over the suit land which is not legally tenable. He further submits that the defendant attained the fraudulent compromised decree in Title Suit No. 78 of 1988 which cannot be the basis of his title. The learned trial Court dismissed the suit of the plaintiff merely on technical ground that the plaint was not properly prepared. Finally, he submits that since there is no non-reading, misreading and non-consideration of material evidence on record the finding of the lower appellate Court is not liable to be disturbed by the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>15. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, exhibits, registered deed, documents and also the judgment of both the Courts below it appears that the trial Court discussed the evidence and also perused the documents and legal aspect of the case and made his observation that the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned trial Court further held in his judgment that since PWs 2 and 3 admitted the possession of the defendant in the suit land the plaintiff ought to have sought for recovery of khas possession as consequential relief. But the plaintiff instituted a simple suit for declaration of title which is not maintainable and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria while reversing the judgment of the trial Court did not write a single word about this specific finding of the law point by the trial Court which appears to be manifestly perverse. Moreover, when the plaintiff No. 2 during the pendency of the suit in the trial Court by submitting a compromise petition relinquished his claim over 20 decimals of the suit land then the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 3 ought to have amended the schedule of the suit land but the plaintiffs did not do so. This observation made by the trial Court was absolutely correct but the lower appellate Court did not at all consider this vital and material point and did not mention anything in his judgment on this point. The lower appellate Court while reversing the judgment of the trial Court is required to reverse the material finding of the trial Court with reference to the evidence on record but the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria did not do so. The lower appellate Court should assign cogent and reasonable ground in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Ranajit Sarker vs Sree Sukhendu Bikash Biswas reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 58 = 2 BLC (AD) 100 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"Order XLI rule 31</u>

<u>Judgment of Reversal</u>

<u>"The appellate Court failed to advert to the specific reasoning’s of the trial Court nor did it discuss all the material evidence taken into consideration by the trial Court. The gross omission made by the appellate Court is in respect of the clear findings by the trial Court about the deed of agreement for reconveyance and the subsequent deeds of sale as genuine. This goes to the root of the merit of the case. Since no relief could be granted to the plaintiffs without coming to any finding that any of the said deeds other than the deeds of sale under pre-emption were sham transaction, the appellate Court was wrong in reversing the judgment of the trial Court in a casual manner".</u>

16. The impugned judgment of the trial Court it transpires, that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered the material evidence and facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal aspect with regard to the maintainability of the case. The learned trial Court did not commit any error of law and illegality in arriving at its finding because the plaintiff could not prove the possession in the suit land by adducing oral evidence. The lower appellate Court committed an error of law and came to a wrong finding occasioning failure of justice in not considering the possession of the defendant over the suit land which was the material fact of the case affecting the merit of the case and, as such, committed error of law which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In this connection I like to refer the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowdhury vs Md Nurul Amin reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein it has been held:

"If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case."

17. In view of the facts and legal position of the case I find that the lower appellate Court is absolutely wrong in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court and, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court is liable to be set aside.

18. The discussion made above and the facts and legal position of the case, the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-1-2006 and 7-2-2006 respectively passed by the learned District Judge, Brahmanbaria, in Title Appeal No. 7 of 2005 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 16-10-2004 and 21-10-2004 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kashba, Brahmanbaria, in Title Suit No. 28 of 2004 dismissing the suit is hereby set aside and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is hereby affirmed.

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to the costs.

20. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Lower Court's record be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.
