case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3-4-2004 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave Appeal No. 1075 of 2003.)
full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha J: In this appeal leave was granted to consider the questions as to whether this Division has committed any error apparent on the face of the judgment in CP No. 1075 of 2003 in maintaining the judgment of the High Court Division which has affirmed the decree for compensation at the rate of Taka 5,000 per day from the date of termination of the tenancy by legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act while passing a decree for ejectment and secondly, whether in the absence of sufficient pleadings, prayer, evidence and findings in support of compensation, the court has power to pass such decree.

2. Facts are shortly narrated as under. Respondents instituted a regular suit in the Civil Court for ejectment of the appellant from the suit premises on the ground of default in paying monthly rents. Appellant, a school, contested the suit claiming that it was not a defaulter the monthly rents were being deposited regularly in a rent control suit on their refusal to accept the same. The trial Court observed that the appellant was a defaulter; that the period of lease in respect of the suit premises expired on 10th March, 2001 and accordingly, decreed the suit. While passing the decree, it also directed that—

এতদসঙ্গে বিবাদী উক্ত তারিখের মধ্যে বিগত ১০-৩-২০০১ইং তারিখ হইতে বাদী পক্ষের দাবীকৃত ক্ষতি পূরণ আদায় না করিলে বাদীপক্ষ আদালতযোগে বিধি মোতাবেক উক্ত ক্ষতিপূরণের টাকা আদায় করিয়া লইবার অধিকারী রহিলেন।

3. The above direction suggested that while passing the decree for ejectment, it also decreed compensation but the amount of compensation had not been specified and stated that the amount would be calculated and recovered on the basis of the respondents' claim, if not paid in the meantime. The trial Court did not make any finding on the point of sustaining any loss or damage by the respondents due to the appellant's remaining in possession as tenant in the premises. In the operating part of the judgment, it was directed that the appellant shall vacate the premises within 25th November, 2002, failing which, it was further directed that the respondents would be entitled to possession through the process of the court. The High Court Division maintained the decree in its entirety. Appellant then moved a leave petition in this Division which also affirmed the judgment of the High Court Division.

4. Admittedly no prayer was made in the plaint seeking a decree for awarding compensation. Even no foundation was laid in the plaint on the point of claiming compensation. Naturally, no issue was framed on the point of compensation and no finding was also made by the trial Court. In the legal notice, Ext-7, issued on behalf of the respondents determining the tenancy, it was pointed out that 'you are requested to deliver the vacant possession of the premises on 1-2-1999 to my client(s) or their representatives failing which legal action would be taken against you and you would be charged a sum of Taka 5,000 per diem by your illegal occupation of the tenanted premises'. On a cursory glance of the trial Court's judgment it may be presumed that it passed the decree on the assumption that since the appellant did not vacate the premises as per demand of the respondents in their legal notice and since the period of tenancy expired, the respondents are entitled to compensation on the basis of their claim made in the legal notice.

5. In the High Court Division it was argued on behalf of the appellant that the direction given on the question of compensation was beyond the power of the Court. The High Court Division did not address the point and maintained the decree observing: 'the trial Court committed no illegality in decreeing the suit and the impugned judgment and decree do not call for any interference by this Court'. In course of hearing of the leave petition, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant submitted that the appellant agitated in the High Court Division that it was not liable to pay damage of Taka 5,000 per day for staying in the suit premises even after expiry of lease the learned Judges of the High Court Division seriously erred in law in not deciding the point though noticed in the judgment... In course of the hearing of the leave petition as well, it was urged that 'the petitioner (appellant) is not liable to pay damage of Taka 5,000 a day for staying in the premises even after expiry of the lease....' and thus, a serious injustice has been caused to the petitioner'. This Division did not deal with the point and affirmed the judgment of the High Court Division.

6. It was urged on behalf of the appellant that in the absence of pleadings, prayer, evidence and findings on the question of compensation, this Division has committed error of law in maintaining the judgment of the High Court Division so far as it relates to the decree for compensation. Learned counsel appearing for the respondents finds it difficult to repel the contention and argues that the trial Court, in fact has not passed any decree for compensation and that the respondents are also not claiming any such compensation.

7. This admission of the learned counsel is sufficient to dispose of the appeal but the operating part of the judgment as quoted above shows otherwise. Moreso, the materials on record reveal that the respondents are really and in fact claiming compensation on the basis of the direction given in the operating part of the judgment of the trial Court and the trial Court has drawn up decree accordingly. The appellant has enclosed the copy of the decree drawn up by the trial Court on 7th October, 2002 by filing an additional paper book wherein the trial Court reproduced the words used in the operating part of the decree in verbatim. Naturally, if this decree on the question of compensation remains, there would arise various complications if the respondents proceed, with the execution proceeding. There is, therefore, need for examining the point in controversy despite the submission of the learned counsel for the respondents.

8. In the judgment, the High Court Division observed that after the dismissal of Rent  Case No. 15 of 1998, the appellant did not pay rent; that he is therefore, not entitled to get any protection from being evicted as a tenant and that the lease agreement having expired after March, 2001, the appellant was no longer a tenant under the respondents. This Division has reproduced the above observations of the High Court Division and dismissed the petition without meeting the point argued. Therefore, we find substance in the contention of the learned counsel that the High Court Division as well as this Division protanto affirmed the decree for compensation as claimed by the respondents in their legal notice. Now the question that calls for consideration is under what circumstances can a Court pass decree or order, for awarding compensation to a party to the suit. In this connection section 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure is relevant for resolving the point in dispute, which reads:

"95.(1) Where, in any suit in which an arrest of attachment has been effected or a temporary injunction granted under the last proceeding (sic) (preceding) section-

a) it appears to the Court that such arrest, attachment or injunction was applied for on insufficient grounds,

(b) the suit of the plaintiff fails and it appears to the Court that there was no reasonable or probable ground for instituting the same, the defendant may apply to the Court, and the Court may, upon such application, award against the plaintiff by its order such amount, not exceeding [ten thousand] Taka, as it deems a reasonable compensation to the defendant for the expense or injury caused to him; provided that a Court shall not award, under this section, an amount exceeding the limits of its pecuniary jurisdiction.

(2) An order determining any such application shall bar any suit for compensation in respect of such arrest, attachment or injunction."

9. The words taka 'ten thousand' have been substituted for the words 'one thousand by the Code of Civil Procedure (Third Amendment) Act, 2003. What we find from a plain reading of this section is that it is a summary remedy for getting compensation where a temporary injunction or an order of arrest or an order of attachment of the property before judgment has been made under section 94 if such prayers were made on insufficient grounds or there were no reasonable or probable grounds for claiming such reliefs. The defendant in such a proceeding can present a petition to give compensation. The remedy for such claims provided in the section is optional to the person aggrieved. The affected person can also file a regular suit for compensation against the person who sought an injunction/attachment/ arrest etc. on malicious ground if he has not already sought relief under the aforesaid provision. It is thus apparent that this is an alternative remedy in cases of wrongful obtainment of such orders, if any, and it does not in any way interfere with the principles regulating suits for damages for torts-of malicious legal process. As a general principle, where two remedies are available under law one of them should not be taken as operating in derogation of the other.

10. If a party has chosen to pursue one remedy, he cannot afterwards of his failing therein proceed under another provision. A regular suit for damages/compensation is not barred by the omission to proceed under the summary procedure provided in section 95 but, if an application is made and disposed of, such disposal would operate as a bar to regular suit whatever may be the result. The regular suit is based on tort for abusing the process of the Court. In a suit for compensation based on tort the plaintiff is required to prove want of reasonable or probable cause for obtaining injunction or attachment and also that the defendant was affected by malice which is an improper motive.

<u>11. A distinction can be drawn between acts done without judicial sanction and acts done under judicial sanctions improperly obtained. Proof of malice is not necessary when the property to, a stranger, not a party to the suit, is taken in execution but if the plaintiff bringing a suit for malicious legal process is a party to a suit proof of malice is necessary. The plaintiff must prove special damage. The claim of a person for damages for wrongful attachment of property or injunction can fall under two heads- (1) trespass and (2) malicious legal process. Where property belonging to a person, not a party to the suit is wrongly attached, the action is really one grounded on trespass. But where the act of attachment complained of was done under judicial sanction, though at the instance of party, the remedy is an action for malicious legal process. In the case of malicious legal process of Court, the plaintiff has to prove absence of probable and reasonable cause. In cases of trespass the plaintiff has only to prove the trespass and it is for the defendant to prove a good cause or excuse. In the former case the plaintiff has to prove malice on the part of the defendant while in the latter case it is not necessary. Similar views have been expressed in Bank of India vs Lakshmani Dass, AIR 2000 SC 1172. None of the above conditions are applicable in this case, even if it is assumed that there are findings in support of awarding compensation.</u>

12. So, the respondents could claim compensation not exceeding taka one thousand when the suit was instituted in 1999 provided they fulfilled the conditions set out in section 95. If the defendant chose to avail the forum provided in section 95, he was required to establish the ingredients referred to in the section and no more. Sub-section (2) bars a litigant who makes an application from instituting a suit for the same purpose. In case of attachment it is incumbent upon the applicant to prove affirmatively that the attachment was applied for on insufficient ground. The words 'on sufficient grounds' must be taken to mean 'without reasonable or probable cause'. The appellant did not secure an order of attachment of the suit premises and therefore, the respondents could not claim compensation on this ground. Similarly, the respondents were not arrested on the prayer of the appellant and therefore, they are not entitled to compensation.

13. If an injunction was applied for on insufficient ground or the suit of the plaintiff failed, and if it appeared to the Court that there was no reasonable or probable ground for instituting the suit, the Court could in an appropriate case pass order of compensation. Though the appellant instituted Title Suit No. 49 of 1999 for permanent injunction against the respondent and lost-up to this Division in Civil Petition No. 274 of 2001, the respondents did not file any petition in the trial Court for awarding compensation pursuant to the dismissal of the suit for injunction. They also did not file any independent suit for damages or compensation after the dismissal of the suit for injunction. Section 95 does not authorize a defendant to claim compensation against his tenant on the ground of overstaying in possession of the premises after the termination of tenancy or the expiry of the period of tenancy.

<u>14. The compensation can only be paid for such expense, or injury which the claimant suffered by reason of arrest or attachment or injunction. It follows that the claimant has to plead in his petition or in the plaint that by reason of such order he has suffered loss or expense or injury, for which, he claims compensation. He is also required to prove the same by evidence. General damages may be awarded in cases where an order of injunction is obtained on insufficient grounds and there is damage to the credit and reputation of the claimant. It must be established that the damage or loss or malice must be proximate result of the order of injunction. There is nothing on record to come to the conclusion that the actions of the appellant were founded on what is called an abuse of the process of the Court' or malicious proceedings. They are also required to make positive statements in the pleadings and prove that the abuse of the process of the court was malicious. They must also prove want of reasonable and probable cause for claiming damages or compensation.</u>

15. Therefore, there is apparent error in the judgment of this Division in maintaining the decree for compensation. The impugned judgment so far as it relates to maintaining the decree for compensation is required to be reviewed. The words-

এতদসঙ্গে বিবাদী উক্ত তারিখের মধ্যে বিগত ১০-৩-২০০১ইং তারিখ হইতে বাদী পক্ষের দাবীকৃত ক্ষতি পূরণ আদায় না করিলে বাদীপক্ষ আদালযোগে বিধি মোতাবেক উক্ত ক্ষতিপূরণের টাকা আদায় করিয়া লইবার অধিকারী রহিলেন।

16. Wherever appear in the judgment and the decree are hereby expunged.

The appeal is disposed of with the above expunction without, however, any order as to costs.

End.

parties:
GM, Bangladesh Railway ------  Appellant 
vs 
Sajeda Begum and ors ------  Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Arayesuddin J: This appeal, at the instance of plaintiff-appellant General Manager, Bangladesh Railway, has been preferred against the judgment and decree, dated 30-11-1994, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Second Court, Gazipur, in Title Suit No. 136 of 1994, dismissing the same on contest without cost.

2. Short fact necessary to dispose of this appeal, in brief, is that the present appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 94 of 1993 in the Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Gazipur, against the present respondents for declaration of plaintiffs title in the suit property together with the prayer that the ex parte judgment and decree, dated 24-9-1984, passed by the then learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 279 of 1970, is collusive, fraudulent, ineffective and the same is not binding upon the plaintiff and the suit land has not been acquired in LA Case Nos. 62/1964-65 and 14/1965-66 by defendant No. 4. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing joint written statement. The learned trial Court by the impugned judgment dated 30-11-1994, dismissed the suit.

3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree, plaintiff-appellant has preferred this appeal alleging that the impugned judgment and decree is bad in law as well as in facts. The learned Subordinate Judge failed to appreciate the facts and circumstances of the case and also failed to apply his judicial mind in the records and dismissed the suit by making out a third case. The finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff-appellant has got no title in the suit land is not based on fact and the evidences on the record. To that effect plaintiff-appellant has submitted the CSSA and RS Khatians of the suit land which stands in the name of the Railway Authority. These documentary evidences have been overlooked by the learned trial Court. The finding of the trial Court that the suit is barred by limitation is erroneous. The Trial Court travelled beyond its jurisdiction and the finding that the defendant-respondents are entitled to claim compensation is illegal and not supported by any evidence as illegal possessors cannot get compensation for the land possessed by them. The finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff-respondents are entitled to compensation is without any basis as the suit land has not been acquired in LA Case Nos. 62/1964-65 and 14/1965-66.

4. In this appeal, the point for determination is, whether the learned trial Court erred in law to dismiss the suit filed by the present appellant claiming that the judgment and decree, dated 24-9-1984, passed in Title Suit No. 279 of 1970 is collusive, fraudulent, ineffective and the same is not binding upon the plaintiff who has got title in the suit land.

5. On behalf of the appellant, the learned Advocate Mr Shaheed Alam submitted that the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court is ineffective, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff-appellant Bangladesh Railway, as the plaintiff filed the suit claiming that they have 16 annas right, title and interest in the suit land and they are legally entitled to receive proper compensation of LA Case Nos. 62/1964-65 and 14/1965-66. He submitted that in those two Land Acquisition cases the suit land claimed by the respondents has not been acquired by the Government for the Railway Authority. So, the question of payment of compensation does not arise at all. He further submitted that total area of suit plot No. 121 is 5.54 acres. Respondents filed Title Suit No. 279 of 1970 claiming the entire land of that plot. But subsequently, they amended their prayer and claimed 4'94 acres. The amendment petition has been allowed and necessary amendment has been made in the plaint. So, he submitted that Court cannot pass decree for an unspecified portion of land. Lastly, he submitted that the suit filed by the respondents as plaintiffs being a suit for simple declaration without any consequential relief, two kinds of relief cannot be granted and such suit is hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

6. On behalf of the respondents, the learned Senior Counsel Mr TH Khan submitted that the present Title Suit No. 94 of 1993 filed by the appellant is hopelessly barred by limitation, since the appellant was all along aware of the judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 279 of 1970. To that effect he has drawn our attention to the findings made by the trial Court in issue No. 2 wherein the trial Court by referring the specific legal notice 'Exhibit Kha' received by the present plaintiff who on 10-6-1985 wrote a letter to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA). Dhaka intimating him of the aforesaid judgment and decree (Exhibit 'Dha'). Under such circumstances, the Learned Counsel submitted that the period of limitation under Article 95 of the Limitation Act to set aside a judgment and decree on the ground of fraud is three years from the date of knowledge. So, he submitted that knowledge of the appellant about the impugned judgment and decree accrued long ago i.e. prior to three years of the specified period. Accordingly, he submitted that without overcoming the point of limitation the appellant cannot get any relief. On that point, the learned Advocate Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, who also appears on behalf of the respondents, referred Section 3 of the Limitation Act which runs thus:

"Subject to the provisions contained in sections 4 to 25 (inclusive), every suit instituted, appeal preferred and application made, after the period of limitation prescribed therefore by the first schedule shall be dismissed, although limitation has not been set up as a defence."

He submitted that this section is mandatory and when a plaint of a suit is presented beyond the period of limitation it is the duty of the Court to check and verify the same and if it is found to be barred by limitation, it is obligatory on the part of the Court to dismiss the suit forthwith by invoking the power of section 3 of the Limitation Act.

<u>7. In this appeal, the point for determination before us is the legality and illegality of the impugned judgment and decree, dated 30-11-1994, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Second Court, Gazipur, in Title Suit No. 136 of 1994. It is admitted that the respondents—Badaruddin Ahmed, Moslehuddin Ahmed and Feroza Begum—as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 279 of 1970 in the Court of the then learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka, That suit was contested by the defendants and the same was dismissed on contest on 24-8-1971. Against that judgment and decree the present respondents filed First Appeal No. 68 of 1972 before this Court and the impugned judgment and decree was set aside and the suit was sent back on remand for fresh trial. After receiving the record by the trial Court, both the parties filed fresh power. Thereafter, on 24-9-1984 the suit has been decreed ex parte. The present appellant has filed this Title Suit No. 94 of 1993 (re-numbered as Title Suit No. 139 of 1994) long after three years and the same is hopelessly barred by limitation. So, the learned trial Court rightly dismissed the suit. In view of that we do not find any merit in this appeal.</u>

8. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgments and decree, dated 30-11-1994, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Second Court, Gazipur, in Title Suit No. 136 of 1994, is hereby affirmed.

Send down the LC records along with a copy of this judgment to the trial Court concerned immediately for information and necessary action.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 7-3-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.5590 and 5539 of 2004).
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: These appeals arise out of the same judgment and therefore they are disposed of by this judgment.

<u>1. Agrani Bank obtained a preliminary decree against writ petitioner Anwarul Bashir Khan and others in Writ Petition No. 5539 of 2005 on 7th May, 2001 in a suit for foreclosure being Mortgage Suit No. 49 of 1997. The decree was made final on 2nd August, 2001 for a sum of Taka 24,97,31,573. In pursuance thereof, the decree holder bank put the decree into execution in Title Execution Case No. 74 of 2001. In the said execution case Anwarul Bashir Khan filed an application under Order XXI, rule 83 of the Code of Civil Procedure for issuing a sale certificate in his favour in order to enable him to repay the decretal amount by selling one of the mortgaged properties situated at Gulshan. The Artha Rin Adalat rejected the prayer by order dated 14th November, 2002. Thereupon he challenged the said order in the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 6891 of 2002. The High Court Division summarily dismissed the writ petition by judgment and order dated 24th November, 2002 with a direction to the executing Court to "allow the petitioner to sell his Gulshan property first by granting necessary certificate to that effect within 3(three) months from the date of granting such certificate and for that the Court shall not be required to return the mortgage deed and/or the title documents to the petitioner before such sale."</u>

2. Pursuant thereto the executing court issued a sale certificate on 4th April, 2004 enabling the judgment debtor to make the proposed sale of the mortgaged property. It was claimed that the judgment debtor entered into an agreement with Ragib Ali, the respondent No. 1 in Civil Appeal No. 106 of 2006, for transfer of the said mortgaged property at a consideration of Taka 1,95,00,000 on 16 June. 2004 and a sale deed was also executed on 7th July, 2004. Ragib Ali in turn prayed in the executing Court for confirmation of the sale and to accept the value. In the meantime one Kutub Uddin, the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 108 of 2008, filed an application expressing his eagerness to purchase the mortgaged property at Taka 4,00,46,250. The executing Court rejected the Ragib Ali's application and accepted the offer of Kutub Uddin. Kutub Uddin thereupon obtained a deed and prayed for delivery of possession. At this stage the judgment debtor moved Writ Petition No. 5539 of 2004 and Ragib Ali also moved Writ Petition No. 5590 of 2004 against that order. The High Court Division heard both the writ petitions analogously and made the rules absolute without, however, making any direction and/or making any declaration in terms of the rules. The decree-holder Agrani Bank and Kutub Uddin Ahmed thereupon sought leave from the judgment of the High Court Division. The leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was justified in making the rule absolute relying upon the judgment passed in earlier Writ Petition No. 6891 of 2002 which was apparently made in contravention of Order XXI, rule 83 (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and also in violation of the principle of natural justice, inasmuch as, the direction was made without affording the Agrani Bank any opportunity of being heard.

3. The High Court Division observed that the earlier direction made by the High Court Division having not been challenged before this Division and in pursuance of that direction a sale deed having been registered, the executing Court fell in an error in not according permission of the sale in favour of Ragib Ali, and that too, without canceling the sale deed in accordance with law. It has further been observed that Ragib Ali has acquired right in the property and such right cannot be denied since he has purchased the property with prior permission of the Court; that the sale certificate reached its finality; that the acceptance of Kutub Uddin offer for purchase of the same property was also without jurisdiction and that the executing Court was under obligation to accept the sale of the mortgaged property in favour of Ragib Ali.

4. It is argued on behalf of the Agrani Bank that the bar imposed in sub-rule (3) of rule 83 of Order XXI denudes the jurisdiction of the Court or in the alternative, takes away the power of the Court to issue certificate to the judgment debtor for private sale of mortgaged-property; the executing Court is under no obligation to accord permission for sale in favour of Ragib Ali. On the other hand, it is urged on behalf of Kutub Uddin that the facts revealed that as the transaction between the judgment debtor and Ragib Ali is far from being bonafide, the High Court Division committed fundamental error in interfering with the order of sale made in favour of Kutub Uddin which was made with prior permission of the Court and that as the price was much higher than the price said to have been offered by Ragib Ali, the High Court erred in law in not affirming the executing Court's order of sale of the mortgaged property in his favour.

<u>5. When the judgment-debtor prayed for issuance of the sale certificate, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 was in force under the said Ain, the Artha Rin Adalat was empowered to exercise all powers given to a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. Naturally, the provisions of the Code were applicable to a proceeding of the Artha Rin Adalat so far as they were not inconsistent with the Ain. There was no provision under the repealed Ain to issue any sale certificate of the mortgaged property in favour of a judgment-debtor. Order XXI, rule 83(1) provided for postponement of the sale for enabling the judgment-debtor to raise money for payment of the total amount by way of mortgage or lease or private sale of the property with the permission of the Court. The expression, the amount of the decree may be raised used in sub-rule (1) means the total decretal amount and not an amount which could not satisfy the decree, and no Court can grant such permission unless the entire debt can be realized by private alienation. This provision should be read subject to the provision of sub-rule (3) which is a non-obstante clause, which provides "Nothing in this rule shall be deemed to apply to a sale of property directed to be sold in execution of decree for sale in enforcement of a mortgage of, or charge on, such property".</u>

6. So, sub-rule (1) does not apply to cases in which property is directed to be sold in execution of a decree on a mortgage. This is because, the decree holder or the creditor's right of sale, rests on the decree. If the judgment-debtor effected the alienation with the consent of the decree-holder, the implication of such sale would be otherwise. This is because by giving consent to the private sale the decree-holder does not become a holder of the decree for payment of money which is an essential condition for the applicability of section 73 of the Code. Therefore, there is no doubt that in case of a decree for foreclosure, be it the High Court Division, or any other superior Court, it has no power to issue certificate to alienate the mortgaged property for enabling the judgment-debtor to raise money for payment of the total decretal amount by private sale without the consent of the decree holder. The High Court Division had totally overlooked this bar and erroneously directed for the issuance of sale certificate in favour of the judgment-debtor. The direction was also exercised without affording the decree-holder bank an opportunity to defend the order and therefore, this order had no sanctity of law and the decree holder —as not bound by the said direction. Similarly, no right, title and interest in respect of the mortgaged property was conferred upon the purchaser Ragib Ali on the strength of the deed which was allegedly executed by the judgment debtor on the strength of an illegal sale certificate; it was issued in total violation of law.

7. True, the executing Court issued a sale-certificate in favour of the judgment-debtor but that was made on the basis of the direction given by the superior court which direction was made ignoring the provisions of law applicable to the case. Under such circumstances, the executing Court had no other alternative but to follow the said direction. Since the direction was made violating the provisions of law, it had no force of law. Therefore, we find force in the contention made on behalf of the decree-holder bank that the direction being per-incursion, it was not binding upon the decree-holder as well as the executing Court. This transaction of sale was made collusively, which is apparent from the fact that it was sold at Taka 1,95,00,000 against the total decretal amount of Taka 24,97,31,573. Even if it is assumed that only one property was sold leaving aside the other two properties, in view of sale of the same property at Taka 4,00,46,250 during the relevant time it is apparent that the market value of the property was much higher than the amount shown in the deed.

<u>8. There is no doubt that the executing Court without following the procedures for sale of the mortgaged property accepted the offer of Kutub Uddin and a sale deed was also executed and registered in his favour. Learned counsel failed to satisfy us the modus operandi of the order of the Court in accepting his offer. Though we agree with the High Court Division that the acceptance of Kutub Uddin offer was without any sanction of law, we are unable to accept the other observation that the executing Court should have proceeded in compliance the parameters set by it. There is no doubt that the appellant Kutub Uddin Ahmed is a stranger purchaser of the mortgaged property. The executing court accepted his offer ignoring the statutory provision of law for selling mortgaged property in auction.</u>

<u>9. The sales in favour of both Ragib Ali and Kutub Uddin were made violating the law. The High Court Division therefore erred in law in accepting the sale in favour of Ragib Ali while rejecting the other sale in favour of Kutub Uddin. The proper course would have been to sell the mortgaged property in accordance with section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Accordingly, we set-aside the impugned judgment and expunge the direction given by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 6891 of 2002. The sale deeds executed in favour of Ragib Ali and Kutub Uddin Ahmed are hereby cancelled and the executing Court is directed to communicate a copy of the judgment to the concerned Sub-Register's office for taking necessary steps in the light of this judgment. The Artha Rin Adalat is further directed to sell the mortgaged property in accordance with section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.</u>

These appeals are disposed of with the above observations without any order as to costs.

End.
