case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 19th day of January, 2011 passed by the High Court Division Writ Petition No. 363 of 2009)
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated the 19th day of January, 2011 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 363 of 2009 making the Rule absolute.

<u>2. Facts necessary for disposal of this leave petition are that respondent No. 1 as writ-petitioner (hereinafter referred to as the writ-petitioner) filed the writ petition before the High Court Division calling in question the propriety of order No. 99 dated 11-1-2009 passed by the Joint District Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj in Mortgage Execution Case No. 59 of 1994 rejecting the application filed under section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (the Ain, 2003) for cancellation of the auction sale held on 10-11-2008 and allowing him to give chance to repay the loan amount.</u>

3. From the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, it appears that several supplementary affidavits also were filed by the writ-petitioner in support of his case.

4. The case of the writ-petitioner as made out in the writ petition and in the  supplementary affidavits was that he took loan of Taka 11,87,000 (Eleven Lakh Eighty Seven Thousand) only from writ-respondent No. 2, Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, respondent No. 3 herein (hereinafter referred to as the Corporation), in 1979 for construction of a multistoried building on his land measuring 18 decimals situated within Narayangonj town and with that loan money, the writ-petitioner constructed a four storied building on that land and had been living there with his family. As security of that loan, the writ-petitioner mortgaged the said building along with the land to the Corporation. The writ-petitioner failed to repay the loan as per stipulation and consequently, the Corporation filed Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1989 before the District Judge, Narayangonj under article 27 of Bangladesh Housing Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 (PO No. 7 of 1973) against the writ-petitioner. Subsequently, Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1989 was transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj for disposal and it was registered as Artha Rin Mortgage Suit No.152 of 1991. Eventually, the mortgaged suit was decreed. The Corporation as decree-holder levied Mortgage Execution Case No. 59 of 1994 before the Artha Rin Adalat for execution of the decree by selling the mortgaged property in auction. In the execution case, the writ-petitioner appeared and entered into agreement with the decree-holder-corporation and the execution case was disposed of in terms of the solenama filed by both the parties. But as the writ-petitioner failed to repay the outstanding loan as per terms and conditions of the solenama the said execution case was revived on the prayer of the decree-holder-corporation and eventually, the mortgaged property was put in auction on 10-11-2008. In the auction, three bidders participated of whom the added writ-respondent No. 3, Md Selim Hossain, petitioner (hereinafter referred to as auction purchaser-petitioner) became the highest bidder at Taka 28,00,000 (Twenty Eight Lakh) only. The decree-holder-corporation filed an application before the executing Court praying for cancelling the auction sale on the ground of low price. The application was rejected. Thereafter, on 24-11-2008, the writ-petitioner filed an application under section 57 of the Ain, 2003 praying for cancellation of the auction sale stating, inter alia, that the decree-holder-corporation, had already allowed reschedulement for payment of the outstanding loan and he had been paying the loan money according to that reschedulement; after re-schedulement, the writ-petitioner paid a big chunk of money to the decree-holder-corporation, but it without intimating anything to the writ-petitioner revived the execution case and behind his back sold the property in auction at Taka 28,00,000 (Twenty Eight Lakh) only on 10-11-2008 though the property is valued at Taka 1 (one) crore; the actual price of the property in question was initially assessed by the decree-holder-corporation at Taka 87,00,000 (Eighty Seven Lath) and the same was accepted by the Artha Rin Adalat by order dated 10-8-2005. The application was rejected by the Artha Rin Adalat by the order dated 11-1-2008. The decree-holder-corporation filed an application under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for cancellation of the auction sale. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 2008. The Artha Rin Adalat dismissed the miscellaneous case. Against that, the decree-holder-corporation filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 6 of 2009 before the District Judge, Narayangonj which was pending. In the above background, the writ-petitioner filed the writ petition.

5. The main contention raised in the writ petition was that the decree passed in Artha Rin Mortgage Suit No. 152 of 1991 by the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj was without jurisdiction and, as such, a nullity since it had no jurisdiction to try a case filed under article 27 of PO No. 7 of 1973, the decree passed in the Artha Rin Mortgage Suit was not executable at all and therefore, the execution case in question was illegal and the auction held therein and the impugned order along with all other orders passed in that execution case were of no legal effect.

6.Writ-respondent No. 2, decree-holder-corporation, filed an affidavit-in-opposition praying for making the Rule absolute stating that the value of the property in question was Taka 28,00,000, but it was sold in auction at Taka 28,00,000 only which was shockingly low. The respondent filed a miscellaneous case before the Artha Rin Adalat praying for setting aside the auction sale on the ground of low price, but that miscellaneous case was dismissed and against the order of dismissal the respondent filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 6 of 2009 before the District Judge, Narayangonj which was pending for disposal.

7. Auction purchaser-writ-respondent contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition and also by filing several supplementary affidavits-in-opposition. This respondent denied the material case and all the allegations of the writ petitioner and contended that there was no illegality either in the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin Mortgaged Suit No. 152 of 1991 or in the execution case started on the basis of the said decree or in the auction sale of the mortgaged property. The auction sale was held in accordance with law and there was no reason at all for setting aside the same and the impugned order did not suffer from any illegality.

8. A Division Bench of the High Court Division on hearing the Rule by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute declaring the proceedings of Mortgage Execution Case No. 59 of 1994 of the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj and the auction sale of the mortgage property in question held in the execution case illegal. The High Court Division further directed that the possession of the mortgage property in question be restored to the writ petitioner. The High Court Division further observed that the auction purchaser, (writ-respondent No. 3), would get return of the entire auction money deposited by him.

9. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order, the auction purchaser has filed this leave petition.

10. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Counsel, appearing for the auction purchaser-petitioner, has submitted that the auction sale in question took place on 10-11-2008, the sale certificate was executed and registered on 12-1-2009 and the possession of the auction sold property was delivered to the auction purchaser on 20-1-2009 at about 11-30 am and since then he has been in possession thereof. Thus, the auction sale had already taken its full effect and there remained nothing to be done in respect of the same. The High Court Division fell into an error in setting aside the auction sale. He has further submitted that the writ-petitioner himself appeared in the Artha Rin Mortgage Suit in question and he never raised any objection as to the jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat in hearing and disposing of the suit and also appeared in the execution case long before and admitting the decree as valid one entered into an agreement with the decree-holder-corporation to pay the decretal amount, but he failed to make the payment as per the terms of the agreement and thereafter the auction was held in accordance with law, he was estopped to challenge the auction sale and there was no scope to set-aside the same which the High Court Division failed to consider in passing the impugned judgment and order. Mr Alam has lastly submitted that the auction purchaser is a bonafide purchaser and he, besides paying the auction money to the tune of Taka 28,00,000 (Twenty Eight Lakh), had to incur expenses on other counts such as: registration fee, gain tax and courts fees @ 2%, but the High Court Division, while declaring the mortgage execution case and the auction sale illegal, only observed that the auction purchaser would get return of the entire auction money to his great prejudice and financial loss and therefore, the impugned judgment and order calls for interference by this Court by way of giving leave.

11. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel, appearing for the judgment debtor-respondent, on the other hand, has submitted that the proceedings under article 27 of PO No. 7 of 1973 being not a suit as already decided by this Division in the case of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation vs Jahanara Akhtar, 49 DLR (AD) 80, the Artha Rin Adalat had no jurisdiction to hear the same by registering it as an Artha Rin Mortgage suit; the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin Mortgage Suit No.152 of 1991 was without jurisdiction and thus, was a nullity, the High Court Division rightly declared both the mortgage execution case in question and the auction sale held therein illegal and as such, no interference is called for with the impugned judgment and order and the leave petition be dismissed. Mr Islam has further submitted that since, in the meantime, the writ-petitioner, the loanee of the decree-holder-corporation, has already paid the entire outstanding dues, the cause of action to proceed with the application filed under article 27 of PO No. 7 of 1973 vide Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1987, no more subsists. Therefore, without reviving the miscellaneous case (16 of 1989), the same may be disposed of finally by this Court invoking the power vested with this Court under article 104 of the Constitution in order to do complete justice and in support of his submission, he has referred to the case of M/s Gannysons Limited vs Sonali Bank, 37 DLR (AD) 43.

12. From the facts of the case and also the finding of the High Court Division, One thing is very clear that Mortgage Execution Case No. 59 of 1994, in which the property in question  was sold in auction, was filed for execution of the decree passed in Artha Rin Mortgage Suit No. 152 of 1991 (hereinafter referred to as the Mortgage suit) and the Mortgage suit arose out of Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1989 filed by the decree-holder-corporation under article 27 of PO No. 7 of 1973 before the District Judge, Narayangonj. This miscellaneous case was transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj pursuant to the provision of section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. In view of the decision of this Division in the case of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation (supra) (the High Court Division relied upon this case), the transfer of the said miscellaneous case to the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj and registration thereof as Mortgage suit was without jurisdiction and the decree passed therein was a nullity and therefore, that was not executable, but that cannot altogether make the Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1989 filed by the decree-holder-corporation a nullity. So far as this miscellaneous case is concerned, there was no procedural defect in filing the same and that was filed in clear compliance with the mandate of the provisions of PO No. 7 of 1973. Factually and legally, the said miscellaneous case needs to be heard afresh as per requirement of law by restoring its position as it stood when it was transferred to the Artha Rin Adalat under section 9 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, but in view of so many intervening facts that in the mortgage suit, the decree was passed by the Artha Rin Adalat on 28-6-1994, the auction sale in question was held on 10-11-2008 in Mortgage Execution Case No. 59 of 1994 levied for execution of the decree passed in the mortgage suit, all the formalities of the auction sale including delivery of possession was completed and in the meantime, the judgment-debtor, writ-petitioner has paid off the entire outstanding dues of the decree-holder-corporation, it does not appear reasonable and practicable to us to take recourse to that procedure. And in fact, by reviving the miscellaneous case to its original position and sending the same for hearing afresh to the District Judge, Narayangonj, no useful purpose shall be served, as the writ-petitioner-loanee against whom the application was filed for realization of the loan amount, has already paid off the entire outstanding loan. This is clear from the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the decree-holder-corporation in the writ petition and also the submission made before the High Court Division as noted in the impugned judgment that "Mr Shahed Alam, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2, Bangladesh Housing Building Finance Corporation has stated before us that the writ petitioner has already paid off the entire outstanding dues of Bangladesh Housing Building Finance Corporation and Bangladesh Housing Building Finance Corporation has no objection in making the Rule absolute."

13. In the case of M/s Gannysons Ltd and another (supra), this Division invoked the power vested under article 104 of the Constitution to do complete justice on the following facts:

"Sonali Bank, respondent No. 1, obtained a decree in Title Suit No. 249 of 1976 for foreclosure and sale of the mortgaged properties belonging to the appellant company and put it into execution in Title Execution No. 46 of 1980. Appellant-company appeared before the Court and prayed for staying the execution of the decree on the grounds that since the Bank proceeded against the appellant Company's properties being treated as abandoned by the Government, the Directors of the appellant Company were not properly, served with notice and that had, therefore, no knowledge of the aforesaid title suit. As a result they did not appear in the suit. Also the Government which was made a party did not take any steps. However, "on the prayer of the appellant Company the proceeding in the execution case was stayed till October 20, 1981. In Writ Petition No. 720 of 1981 a Rule was issued at the instance of the appellant company on October 20, 1981. But it abated on March 24, 1982 after the proclamation of Martial Law. In Miscellaneous Case No. 958 of 1981 which was filed by the appellant Company under section 47 of the Code its prayer against the execution of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 249 of 1976 was disallowed by the Court. The appellant Company's appeal against this order was dismissed by the High Court Division on 9 November 1982. The appellant Company, being aggrieved, moved this Court and succeeded in having the appeal (Civil Appeal No. 43 of 1983) against the order of the trial Court rejecting their objection under section 47 of the Code allowed. Appellants filed review petition against the judgment passed in the civil appeal against the concluding paragraph of the judgment which was as follows:

"Decree dated 27-3-80 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 314 Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 249 of 1976 be stayed for six months and the Miscellaneous Case No. 958 of 1981 pending in the 3rd court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka be struck down." And leave was granted to consider the only ground to the following effect:

"For that consistently with the reasoning’s in the main body of the judgment and the decision allowing the appeal (CA No. 43 of 1983) arising out of Miscellaneous Case No. 958 of 1981 started under section 47 CPC at the instance of M/s Gannysons Ltd. and another) the Title Execution Case No. 46 of 1980 pending in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, needs to be struck down and the said Miscellaneous Case No. 958 of 1981 of the same court allowed and that the order saying the decree dated 27-3-80 in Title Suit No. 279 of 1976 of the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge needs to be deleted."

14. Considering the definition of abandoned property as given in President's Order No. 16 of 1972, it was found that Gannysons Limited Company, in no circumstances, could be declared as an abandoned property, allowed the review application, declared that the property was not an abandoned property, struck down the execution case subject to payment of the decretal amount to the Bank directly by the appellants and directed the Government to release the property treating Title Suit No. 508 of 1982 filed by the appellant as withdrawn being infructuous. In that case, Fazle Munim, CJ observed:

"17. In view of the circumstances above and in virtue of the power conferred upon this Court by the Constitution of Bangladesh, vide Article 104, to do complete justice in a case it is declared that Gannysons Limited is not an abandoned property, it should, therefore, be immediately, released. Along with the release of Gannysons Limited any of its properties, assets and capital should also be released and returned to it."

<u>15. Be that as it may, before we decide whether we shall invoke the power vested in this Court under article 104 of the Constitution in order to do complete justice in this case, we need to answer one point raised by Mr Mahbubey Alam that though the writ-petitioner appeared in the suit and also in the execution case, he did not raise any question about the jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat in disposing of the suit and also the decree passed therein and accepting the decree as a valid one entered into an agreement with the decree-holder-corporation to pay the decretal amount, but failed to pay the decretal amount and then the execution case was revived and the property in question was sold in auction, so he was estopped from raising any objection as to the jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat to hear and dispose of the mortgaged suit in question and the validity of the decree passed therein. Our answer is very simple and is that mere failure to raise objection as to the jurisdiction of a Court to hear and try a suit or a case or in other words, mere surrendering to the jurisdiction of a Court, jurisdiction cannot be conferred to a Court it is found that the Court which heard or disposed of the suit or the case had no jurisdiction to hear such suit or case as the case may be. Because the decree or order passed by a Court without Jurisdiction is a nullity and such nullity, in no way, is curable or immune from being challenged. So, in the instant case, even if the writ-petitioner failed to take any objection against the disposal of the suit by the Artha Rin Adalat, the decree passed therein shall not get the seal of validity or shall not be immuned from attack or being challenged. In the context, the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in declaring the mortgaged execution case in question and the auction sale held therein as illegal.</u>

16. It is also a fact that the auction purchaser-petitioner being the highest bidder at Taka 28,00,000 (Twenty Eight Lakh), his bid was accepted by the executing Court (though the valuation of the property assessed at Taka 87,00,000 by the corporation was accepted by the Artha Rin Adalat by order dated 10-8-2005) and he deposited the entire bid money on 19-11-2008. In ground No. IX of the leave petition, it has been specifically mentioned that besides paying the auction money, the auction purchaser had to incur expenses of Taka 1,38,800 as registration fee, Taka 84,000 as advance income tax and Taka 56,000 as poundage Court fees, which Mr Mahmudul Islam could not dispute. Mr Mahbubey Alam in a separate typed sheet has shown a total of Taka 2,95,576 which included the cost on the above heads plus Taka 1,000, 2000, 13,517 and 259 on the account of fee for Najir for delivery of possession, fee of the Commissioner, conveyance of police force and conveyance of the Magistrate respectively in connection with the auction purchase. Besides, another sum of Taka 26,00,283.83 has been claimed as interest @ 16% on the amount of auction purchased money which the auction purchaser allegedly took as loan from City Bank Limited and Taka 15,00,000 as maintenance costs of the 4(four) storied building since 18-1-2009 till date.

<u>17. Taking into account the entire facts of the case as noted down hereinbefore, the claim of the auction purchaser as to the incurring of expenditure by him incidental to the auction purchase and the legal position that the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat was a nullity, we invoke the power vested in this Court vide article 104 of the Constitution in order to do complete justice in a case and dispose of the leave petition in the following terms:</u>

<u>(i)	The orders of the High Court Division declaring the proceedings of Mortgaged Execution Case No. 59 of 1984 of the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj and the auction sale of the mortgaged property in question held in the said execution as illegal, the observation that "The auction purchaser respondent No. 3 will get return of the entire auction money which he deposited" and the direction that "the possession of mortgaged property in question be restored to the petitioner" are maintained subject to term Nos.(iii) and (iv) mentioned hereinafter.</u>

<u>(ii)	It is declared that Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1989 of the Court of the District Judge, Narayangonj arising out of the application under article 27 of the PO No. 7 of 1973 filed by the House Building Finance Corporation has become infructuous in view of the admitted fact that the writ-petitioner loanee has paid the entire outstanding dues to the House Building Finance Corporation.</u>

<u>(iii)	The writ-petitioner-respondent, Shahabuddin Ahmed, shall pay in total a sum of Taka 2,79,800 to the auction purchaser, Md Selim Hossain, petitioner herein, on the following counts:</u>

<u>(a) Taka 1,38,800 as registration fee,</u>

<u>(b) Taka 84,000, as gain tax fee/advance income tax,</u>

<u>(c) Taka 56,000, as poundage Court fee/ Court fee and</u>

<u>(d) Taka 1,000 (one thousand) as fee for Najir for giving delivery of possession of the mortgage property sold in auction,</u>

<u>(e) Interest at the rate of 10% over the auction money of Taka 28,00,000 (Twenty Eight Lakh) till this day, that is, 3-2-2014.</u>

<u>(iv)	The writ-petitioner, Shahabuddin Ahmed, respondent No. 1 herein, shall make deposit of the amount mentioned hereinbefore (term No. (iii)) in Mortgage Execution Case No. 59 of 1994 of the Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj in the name of the auction purchaser, Md Selim Hossain within two months from the date of receipt of this judgment and he (the auction purchaser) shall be entitled to withdraw the money deposited by the writ-petitioner at once and the executing Court shall do the needful in that respect without causing any delay. 7(seven) days from the date of deposit of the money by the writ-petitioner-respondent as detailed in term No. (iii) herein-before, he shall be entitled to take appropriate steps in the Mortgage Execution Case No. 59 of 1994 to restore back possession of the mortgage property to him and in that case, the auction purchaser shall restore back possession of the auction sold property to the writ-petitioner without creating any hindrance or obstacle and the executing Court shall pass necessary order in that respect.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan with SRM Lutfor Rahman Akand, Advocates--For the Petitioners. 
MA Azim Khair, Deputy Attorney-General--For Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Mahmuda Begum and others ------ Petitioners 
Vs
Chairman, First Court of Settlement and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: This Rule Nisi was issued upon the respondents as to why the impugned Judgment and order dated 26-11-1995 (Annexure-C) passed by the respondent No. 1 should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. Further, Rule was issued upon the respondent No. 2 to show cause as to why the case property being House No. H/11, Block-E, Zakir Hossain Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka enlisted as an abandoned property in the 'Ka' list published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 23-9-1986, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and without Jurisdiction.

2. The respondent No. 2 has contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-oppositions.

3. The petitioners have filed supplementary-affidavits dated 2-10-2005 and 9-1-2005.

4. The case of the petitioners, in short, is that the case property being House No. H/11, Block-E, Zakir Hossain Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka was leased out to the respondent No. 3 Abdul Kaiyum by a registered lease deed dated 6-1-1960 for a period of 99 years and pursuant to the lease, the respondent No. 3 was given delivery of possession of the case property. Thereafter, the respondent No. 3 erected a house on the case property and possessed the same by residing therein along with the members of his family. On 27-12-1970 the respondent No. 3 entered into a contract for sale of the case property with the original petitioner Md Atiqullah (since deceased) for a consideration of Taka 10,000 only On the date of execution of the deed of agreement on 27-12-1970, Md Atiqullah paid a sum of Taka 4000 only to the respondent No. 3 by way of earnest money. Subsequently, on different dates, out of the balance consideration money, the respondent No. 3 received a further sum of Taka 5,300 on the promise of executing and registering the contemplated sale deed. But the respondent No. 3 failed to execute and register the sale deed as agreed upon. As such, Md Atiqullah filed Title Suit No. 395 of 1981 in the First Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka, against said Abdul Kaiyum and others for specific performances of contract. In spite of the service of summons upon the defendants of that suit, they did not enter appearance therein and eventually the said suit being ready for hearing otherwise was decreed ex parte on 30-6-1983. Thereafter Title Execution Case No. 39 of 1983 was filed and Md Atiqullah obtained the contemplated deed of transfer through the Court on 13-9-1983. At the instance of Md Atiqullah, the Executing Court delivered the possession of the case property to him on 27-2-1984 by way of execution of a writ of delivery of possession and since 27-2-1984, Md Atiqullah or, for that matter his legal heirs (present Writ Petitioners) have been living in the case property. Thereafter the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) was promulgated and the case property was illegally enlisted in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23-9-1986 under the authority of the said Ordinance. As against such illegal enlistment of the case property in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings, Md Atiqullah made an application before the First Court of Settlement under section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 on 13-8-1986, which was registered as Settlement Case No. 177 of 1988. As against the ex-parte decree dated 30-6-1983 obtained in Title Suit No. 395 of 1981, the respondent No. 2 preferred Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was ultimately dismissed, However, the Settlement Case No. 177 of 1988 was dismissed by the First Court of Settlement in flagrant violation of the relevant provisions of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 by the Judgment and Order dated 26-11-1995. In view of the aforesaid decree of the civil Court, the First Court of Settlement was not legally justified in dismissing the Settlement Case by the impugned judgment and order. The impugned judgment and order dated 26-11-1995 was passed without lawful authority.

5. In the supplementary affidavit dated 2-1-2005, the writ petitioners have stated that the Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was ultimately dismissed for default by the order dated 6-11-2000 passed by the First Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka. Md Atiqullah suddenly died on 12-1-2003 and the present writ petitioners came to know about the order of dismissal of the said Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 only recently, Be that as it may, that writ petitioners have been in possession of the case property since 27-12-1970 in part performance of the contract. They also got delivery of possession of the case property through the Court as a mere formality and symbolically. Article 9 read with Article 10 of PO No. 16 of 1972 contemplate that any allotment, lease or agreement granted or entered into before the 25th March, 1971 is binding upon the Government in the same way as upon the original owner. In the instant case, the agreement for sale being entered into before 25th March, 1971, i.e. on 27-12-1970, is also binding upon the Government and the right and interest of the writ petitioners in the case property have not been affected by the provisions of PO No. 16 of 1972.

6. In the supplementary affidavit dated 9-1-2005, the writ petitioners have stated that they have been in continuous possession of the case property since 27-12-1970 on the strength of the agreement for sale and in part performance thereof and since 27-2-1984 on the basis of the registered deed of conveyance obtained through the Court, However, the Government by Memo No. section IX /E-162/82 /267 dated 29-2-1984 addressing the writ petitioners as 'Occupants' directed them to make over possession of the case property to the representative of the Superintending Engineer, Abandoned House Circle, 88, Motijheel Dhaka within 10 days. The Government also by Memo No. SEC/12 /E-162 /82 /546 dated 17-12-1987 similarly addressing the writ petitioners as 'resident' directed them to make over possession of the case property by 22-12-1987. Those Memos dated 29-2-1987. The Memos dated 29-2-1984 and 17-12-1987 do not speak about or refer to any allotment of the case property by the Government. Besides, the application of the Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the Government (Annexure-B) shows that the Government addressed the original writ petitioner Md Atiqullah (since deceased) with reference to the case property and the notice of the said Miscellaneous Case was duly served upon him at that address. On 17-12-1987 Md Atiqullah made a prayer to the respondent No 2 for not allotting the case property in favour of anybody stating, inter alia, that is the owner-in-possession of the case property by purchase; but during the pendency of the Settlement Case, the property in question was allotted to one Abdul Motaleb and Sheikh Alam. However, at a subsequent stage, the Government cancelled the allotments granted in their favour. The documents marked as Annexures-H series and annexure-L were placed before the Court of Settlement and the notices marked as Annexure-I and J series were materials on record of the Court of Settlement and these documents show that the Government was not in possession of the case property at any point of time. On the contrary, the writ petitioners have been in possession of the case property all through and the Court of Settlement failed to consider this aspect of possession and illegally dismissed the case by the impugned judgment and order.

7. The case of the respondent No. 2 in the affidavit-in-opposition, in short, is that the case property is under the control and management of the Government and the same was published in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings prepared under the relevant provisions of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. The Court of Settlement, on consideration of the materials on record, came to the finding that the ownership of the case property did not legally pass to the writ petitioners and the original owner Abdul Kaiyum was not available in the country on the date of promulgation of the PO No. 16 of 1972 and his whereabouts were unknown when the Government took effective control of the case property as an abandoned property. Since the case property is an abandoned property by operation of law, it could not be transferred to Md Atiqullah in the year 1983 in view of Article 6 of the PO No. 16 of 1972. The original owner Abdul Kaiyum left the country leaving behind the case property uncared for at the time of promulgation of the PO No. 16 of 1972 and accordingly, the case property assumed the character of an abandoned property and thenceforth the Government has been treating the same as such. The enlistment of the case property in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings is legal and proper. By the impugned Judgment and order dated 26-11-1995, the Court of Settlement legally dismissed the case of the petitioners and maintained the enlistment of the case property in the 'Ka' list. The abandoned character of the case property cannot be questioned by the petitioners in the writ jurisdiction. The petitioners have no right, title and interest in the case property on the basis of the expert decree obtained in Title Suit No. 395 of 1981 of the First Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka, in pursuance of which the transfer deed was executed and registered through the Court. The petitioners are not entitled to get protection under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. The existence of the agreement for sale and the decree of the civil Court are not a bar to the enlistment of the case property as an abandoned property in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings. So, the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

8. We have perused the writ petition, the affidavit-in-opposition and the supplementary affidavits and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties.

9. This writ of certiorari has been filed against the impugned judgment and order of the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka. The High Court Division exercising power under Article 102 of the Constitution does not act as a Court of Appeal and, as such, it is not required to make determination of facts on its own. It can interfere with the findings of a Court of Facts under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 only if it can be shown that the Court has acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence or fact causing prejudice to the complaining party, or it has acted malafide or in violation of the principle of natural justice. In such view of the matter, the scope of enquiry in this Rule with reference to the impugned judgment and order is limited.

10. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that Md Atiqullah went into possession of the case property on 27-12-1970 in part performance of the contract for sale and the suit for specific performance of contract (Title Suit No. 395 of 1981 of the First Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka) having been decreed against the original owner Abdul Kaiyum, the Government and the Abandoned Property Cell, Md Atiqullah got delivery of formal and symbolic possession of the case property through the Court in Title Execution Case No. 39 of 1983 on 27-2-1984 and it is on record that the Government filed Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 395 of 1981; but the said Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 was ultimately dismissed for default and this being the scenario, it cannot be denied that the possession of Md Atiqullah or, for that matter, the present writ petitioners in the case property on the date of execution of the contract for sale, that is to say, on 27-12-1970 is protected by section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. In this connection, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan has referred to the decision in the case of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others vs Kazi Ashrafuddin Ahmed reported in 55 DLR (AD) 16.

11. On the other hand, Mr MA Azim Khair, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 2, submits that it is paragraph 9 of the original writ petition that on the prayer of Md Atiqullah, the Executing Court delivered the possession of the case property in his favour on 27-2-1984 by way of execution of a writ of delivery of possession and since then the writ petitioners have been living in the case property and the alleged possession in the case property by Md Atiqullah on the date of execution of the contract for sale, i.e. on 27-12-1970 is not borne out by the materials on record, save and except the solitary statement made by Md Atiqullah and this being the position, it goes without saying that Md Atiqullah was given delivery of possession of the case property on 27-2-1984 and not prior to that date. Mr MA Azim Khair further submits that as the writ petitioners have filed to prove their possession in the case property since 27-12-1970, they cannot invoke the aid of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. In this context, Mr MA Azim Khair has referred to the decision in the case of Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Dhaka vs Mr KM Zakir Hossain and others reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 24 = 8 BLC (AD) 27.

12. It is the definite assertion of Md Atiqullah that he got delivery of possession of the case property in part performance of the contract on 27-12-1970. This factum of delivery of possession was specifically stated in paragraph 4 of the plaint of Title Suit No. 395 of 1981. Besides, in the supplementary affidavit dated 9-1-2005 the petitioners have stated on oath that they have been in continuous possession of the case property since 27-12-1970 by virtue of the agreement for sale. In the said supplementary affidavit, it has been further stated that since 27-2-1984 the petitioners have been in possession of the case property by dint of the Registered Kabala executed by the Court on behalf of the Judgment-debtor Md. Abdul Kaiyum in favour of Md Atiqullah, However, it is undisputed that the suit for specific performance of contract (Title Suit No. 395 of 1981) was decreed ex parte. In view of the PO No. 142 of 1972, the Government was a party to that suit. Over and above, the record shows that the Abandoned Property Call represented by the concerned property Secretary, Ministry of Works was also made a party to that suit. Admittedly, the Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the Government for setting aside the ex parte decree; but ultimately, the Government did not proceed with the said Miscellaneous case and allowed the same to be dismissed for default as evidenced by Annexure-E to the supplementary affidavit dated 2-1-2005. So, it is easily deducible that the Government had been well-posted about the acquisition of right, title, interest as well as possession of the petitioners in the case property all through.

13. In the case of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others Petitioners vs Kazi Ashrafuddin Ahmed Respondent, referred to above, it has been held that the respondent being in possession of the case property on the basis of an agreement for sale has the protection of the provisions of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. In that case, the agreement for sale was dated 21-4-1968 i.e. prior to 25th March, 1971.

14. In the case of the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works, Dhaka vs Mr KM Zakir Hossain and others reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 24 = 8 BLC (AD) 27 referred to by Mr MA Azim Khair, it has been held that there is no material on record to show that pursuant to the agreement for sale, the respondent No. 1 was inducted into possession of the property before 28-2-1972 and since on and from 28-2-1972 the property vested in the Government the respondent No. 1's possession is not protected under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and in view of the Provisions of section 5(2) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, the respondent No. 1 was required to substantiate his claim of going into possession pursuant to the agreement prior to the promulgation of the PO No. 16 of 1972.

15. According to the case of the respondent No. 2, the case property was enlisted in the 'Ka' list as per provisions of Section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. In other words, it is the assertion of the Government that it took over and continues to be in possession of the case property as an abandoned property, and accordingly included it in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings. But the factual aspect is otherwise. In this perspective, our attention has been drawn to Annexure-H and H(1) annexed to the supplementary affidavit dated 9-1-2005. From a bare reading of those two Annexures, it seems that the Government called upon the 'occupants' or 'residents' of the case property to make over possession of the same within the given time-frame and those notices were served upon the petitioners, who were in actual possession of the case property. Had the Government been really in possession of the case property as claimed, it would not have called upon the 'occupants' 'residents' of the said property to make over possession thereof to the specified persons within the stipulated period. It may be mentioned that the Annexure-H is dated 29-2-1984 and the Annexure H(1) is dated 17-12-1987 Further, the application of the Miscellaneous Case No. 254 of 1986 (Annexure-B) unerringly indicates that the Government gave the address of Md Atiqullah referring to the case property. Nor is this all, a reference to the Annexure-F(1) annexed to the supplementary affidavit dated 2-1-2005 positively shows that Md Atiquallah paid gas bill in respect of the case property on 16-5-1986 i.e. prior to the publication of the Ka list of abandoned building on 23rd September, 1986. From these Annexures we are of the view that the Government did not take over possession of the case property as an abandoned property in accordance with the provisions of Article 7 of the PO No. 16 of 1972. What we are trying to drive at boils down to this, those Annexures B, H and H(1) coupled with Annexure F(1) belie the case of the Government on the question of taking over possession of the case property as an abandoned property.

16. In this Rule, we are also concerned with the abandoned character or otherwise of the case property on the date of promulgation of the PO No. 16 of 1972 i.e. on 28th February 1972. It is admitted that on that date (28-2-1972) the original owner Abdul Kaiyum did not possess the case property in person. The assertion that Md Atiqullah got delivery of possession of the case property in part performance of the contract on 27-12-1970 cannot be brushed aside at all in the facts and circumstances of the case. In view of the agreement for sale dated 27-12-1970 it appears that as an agent of the original owner Abdul Kaiyum, Md Atiqullah possessed the case property also on 28-2-1972 though he acquired valid title thereto in the year 1984 on registration of the kabala through the court. That being so, the claim of the petitioners that on the date of promulgation of the PO No. 16 of 1972 (28-2-1971) the case property was not left abandoned by the original owner Abdul Kaiyum as to attract the mischief of article 2 thereof but they were in possession of the case property on that date has substance, moreso when the Government could not produce any material to prove its possession of the case property at any point of time.

17. Article 10 of PO No. 16 of 1972 however, confers upon the Government some extraordinary powers which are not possessed by the original owner, and which include, inter alia, the power of termination of an agreement. For proper appreciation of the said power of the Government, the provisions of Article 10 of PO No. 16 of 1972 are quoted below verbatim:

"10(1) The Government may cancel any allotment or terminate any lease or amend the terms of any lease or agreement under which any abandoned property is held, occupied or managed by a person. Where such allotment, lease or agreement has been granted or entered into after the 25th March 1971.

(2) Where by reason of any action taken under clause (1) any person has ceased to be entitled to possession of any abandoned property he shall, on demand by the government, surrender possession of such property to the Government or to any person authorized by it in this behalf.

(3) If any person fails to surrender possession of any property on demand under clause (2) the Government may eject such person and take possession of such property in such manner as may be prescribed.

18. From the above provisions of Article 10, it seems to be clear that any allotment or lease of or any agreement relating to an abandoned property is binding upon the Government as custodian subject to its right as conferred under the said provisions. It appears that any allotment, lease or agreement granted or entered into before the 25th March, 1971 is binding upon the Government in the same way as upon the original owner having entered into the shoes of the lawful owner but the allotment agreement or lease granted or entered in to after the 25th March 1971 may be cancelled, terminated or amended by the Government, if it chooses to do so, and if a person is in possession of an abandoned property by virtue of such allotment, lease or agreement can be asked to surrender possession of such property only if the Government cancels or terminates such an allotment, lease or agreement under clause (2) of the Article and as is provided in clause (3) the Government may eject such a person only when he fails to surrender possession under clause (2) of the Article.

19. In the instant Rule, agreement for sale is dated 27-12-1970 i.e. prior to 25th March, 1971. Considered from this standpoint the said agreement dated 27-12-1970 does not come within the purview of Article 10 of the PO No. 16 of 1972 unconditionally but subject to the terms and conditions of the agreement for sale. The provisions of the said Order do not confer any power upon the Government, apart from Article 10, to ignore an agreement entered into after 25-3-1971 and eject the occupant lawfully in possession of the abandoned property.

20. As already observed, the petitioners have been in continuous possession of the case property on the basis of the agreement for sale dated 27-12-1970 and, as such, they have the protection of the provisions of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.

21. Mr MA Azim Khair has next referred to the decision in the case of Hosne Ara Begum vs Chairman, Court of Settlement and another reported in 46 DLR (AD) 9 in support of his submission that so long as the Court of Settlement acts within its jurisdiction and does not commit any excess of jurisdiction, the High Court Division will not interfere therewith, on the ground of mere unsatisfactory disposal of a case.

22. On the contrary, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan submits that the Court of Settlement exceeded its jurisdiction in holding that the writ of delivery of possession is not reliable and that the ownership of the case property did not pass to Md Atiqullah legally in view of the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 395 of 1981. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan further submits that the Court of Settlement virtually acted as a Court of Appeal over the ex parte judgment and decree of the civil Court by making the aforementioned finding which is ex facie illegal and without lawful authority, and consequently the impugned judgment and order of the Court of Settlement cannot be sustained in law.

<u>23. Mr MA Azim Khair has rightly submitted that so long the Court of Settlement acts within its jurisdiction and does not commit any excess of jurisdiction the High Court Division will not interfere on the ground of mere unsatisfactory disposal of a case. Be that us it may, the findings referred to above arrived at by the Court of Settlement as to title and possession in the impugned judgment and order undoubtedly lead as to hold that the said Court exceeded its jurisdiction in assailing the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 395 of 1981 and its effect. To put it differently, the court of Settlement erred in law in casting doubt about the writ of delivery of possession and the passing of title of the case property to Md Atiqullah on the basis of the decree passed a in Title Suit No. 396 of 1981.</u>

24. Section 5(2) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 clearly provides that the lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned properties and have vested in the Government as such.

25. Section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 contemplates that a person claiming any right or interest in any such building may make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of such building as not an abandoned one and it has not vested in the Government under the PO No. 16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that order. The onus, therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government is under no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of the treatment of the property as an abandoned property.

<u>26. In the instant Rule, the writ petitioners have proved their possession in the case property on the basis of the agreement for sale dated 27-12-1970. Their possession in the case property has been continuous, undisturbed and uninterrupted since 27-12-1970 as the agents of the original owner Abdul Kaiyum. Furthermore, the decree of the Civil Court in favour of the writ petitioners was obtained before the promulgation of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. On top of that, the Government did not take over the possession of the case property at least before its inclusion in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings prepared under the authority of the PO No. 16 of 1972 or the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. Against this back-drop, we have no hesitation in holding that the writ petitioners have discharged the onus of proving that the case property is not an abandoned property and the Government included the same in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings illegally. The writ petitioners have also proved their possession in the case property after 1986 in that the notices from the Settlement Court were sent to them at the address of the case property, which were duly served upon them.</u>

27. From the foregoing discussions and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and having regard to the materials on record, we find merit in the Rule.

Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. It is declared that the enlistment of the case property being House No. 8/11, Block-E, Zakir Hossain Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka in the 'Ka' List of abandoned buildings published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23-9-1986 is illegal and without lawful authority and it is further declared that the said case property is not an abandoned property. The respondent No. 2 is directed to exclude the said case property from the aforesaid 'Ka' List of abandoned buildings within 60 days from date.

End.
